New equidistribution estimates of Zhang type

D.H.J. Polymath Address: http://michaelnielsen.org/polymath1/index.php
Abstract.

We prove distribution estimates for primes in arithmetic progressions to large smooth squarefree moduli, with respect to congruence classes obeying Chinese Remainder Theorem conditions, obtaining an exponent of distribution 12+7300\frac{1}{2}+\frac{7}{300}.

1. Introduction

In May 2013, Y. Zhang [52] proved the existence of infinitely many pairs of primes with bounded gaps. In particular, he showed that there exists at least one h≥2h\geq 2 such that the set

{p​ prime ∣p+h​ is prime}\{p\text{ prime }\,\mid\,p+h\text{ is prime}\}

is infinite. (In fact, he showed this for some even hh between 22 and 7×1077\times 10^{7}, although the precise value of hh could not be extracted from his method.)

Zhang’s work started from the method of Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım [23], who had earlier proved the bounded gap property, conditionally on distribution estimates concerning primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli, i.e., beyond the reach of the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem.

Based on work of Fouvry and Iwaniec [11, 12, 13, 14] and Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec [3, 4, 5], distribution estimates going beyond the Bombieri–Vinogradov range for arithmetic functions such as the von Mangoldt function were already known. However, they involved restrictions concerning the residue classes which were incompatible with the method of Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım.

Zhang’s resolution of this difficulty proceeded in two stages. First, he isolated a weaker distribution estimate that sufficed to obtain the bounded gap property (still involving the crucial feature of going beyond the range accessible to the Bombieri--Vinogradov technique), where (roughly speaking) only smooth11 1 I.e, friable. moduli were involved, and the residue classes had to obey strong multiplicative constraints (the possibility of such a weakening had been already noticed by Motohashi and Pintz [43]). Secondly, and more significantly, Zhang then proved such a distribution estimate.

This revolutionary achievement led to a flurry of activity. In particular, the Polymath8 project was initiated by T. Tao with the goal first of understanding, and then of improving and streamlining, where possible, the argument of Zhang. This was highly successful, and through the efforts of a number of people, reached a state in October 2013, when the first version of this paper [46] established the bounded gap property in the form

lim inf(pn+1−pn)≤4680,\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_{n})\leq 4680,

where pnp_{n} denotes the nn-th prime number.

However, at that time, J. Maynard [38] obtained another conceptual breakthrough, by showing how a modification of the structure and of the main term analysis of the method of Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım was able to establish not only the bounded gap property using only the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem (in fact the bound

lim inf(pn+1−pn)≤600\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_{n})\leq 600

obtained was significantly better than the one obtained by Polymath8), but also the bounds

lim inf(pn+k−pn)<+∞\liminf(p_{n+k}-p_{n})<+\infty

for any fixed k≥1k\geq 1 (in a quantitative way), something which was out of reach of the earlier methods, even for k=2k=2. (Similar results were obtained independently in unpublished work of T. Tao.)

Because of this development, a part of the Polymath8 paper became essentially obsolete. Nevertheless, the distribution estimate for primes in arithmetic progressions are not superceded by the new method, and it has considerable interest for analytic number theory. Indeed, it is the best known result concerning primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli without fixing the residue class. (When the class is fixed, the best results remain those of Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec, improving on those of Fouvry and Iwaniec [13, 3].) The results here are also needed to obtain the best known bounds on lim inf(pn+k−pn)\liminf(p_{n+k}-p_{n}) for large values of kk; see [47].

The present version of the work of Polymath8 therefore contains only the statement and proof of these estimates. We note however that some of the earlier version is incorporated in our subsequent paper [47], which builds on Maynard’s method to further improve many bounds concerning gaps between primes, both conditional and unconditional. Furthermore, the original version of this paper, and the history of its elaboration, remain available online [46].

Our main theorem is:

Theorem 1.1.

Let θ=1/2+7/300\theta=1/2+7/300. Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 and A≥1A\geq 1 be fixed real numbers. For all primes pp, let apa_{p} be a fixed invertible residue class modulo pp, and for q≥1q\geq 1 squarefree, denote by aqa_{q} the unique invertible residue class modulo qq such that aq≡apa_{q}\equiv a_{p} modulo all primes pp dividing qq.

There exists δ>0\delta>0, depending only on ε\varepsilon, such that for x≥1x\geq 1, we have

∑q≤xθ−εq xδ-smooth, squarefree|ψ(x;q,aq)−xφ⁡(q)|≪x(log⁡x)A,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq x^{\theta-\varepsilon}\\ q\text{ $x^{\delta}$-smooth, squarefree}\end{subarray}}\Bigl|\psi(x;q,a_{q})-\frac{x}{\varphi(q)}\Bigr|\ll\frac{x}{(\log x)^{A}},

where the implied constant depends only on AA, ε\varepsilon and δ\delta, and in particular is independent of the residue classes (ap)(a_{p}).

In this statement, we have, as usual, defined

ψ⁡(x,q,a)=∑n≤xn=a⁡(q)Λ⁡(n),\psi(x;q,a)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\leq x\\ n=a\ (q)\end{subarray}}\Lambda(n),

where Λ\Lambda is the von Mangoldt function. In [52], Zhang establishes a weaker form of Theorem 1.1, with θ=1/2+1/584\theta=1/2+1/584, and with the aqa_{q} required to be roots of a polynomial PP of the form P⁡(n):=∏1≤j≤k;j≠i(n+hj−hi)P(n):=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k;j\neq i}(n+h_{j}-h_{i}) for a fixed admissible tuple (h1,…,hk)(h_{1},\dots,h_{k}) and i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k.

In fact, we will prove a number of variants of this bound. These involve either weaker restrictions on the moduli (“dense-divisibility”, instead of smoothness, which may be useful in some applications), or smaller values of θ>1/2\theta>1/2, but with significantly simpler proofs. In particular, although the full strength of Theorem 1.1 depends in crucial ways on applications of Deligne’s deepest form of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields, we show that, for a smaller value of θ>1/2\theta>1/2, it is possible to obtain the same estimate by means of Weil’s theory of exponential sums in one variable over finite fields.

The outline of this paper is as follows: in the next section, we briefly outline the strategy, starting from the work of Bombieri, Fouvry, Friedlander, and Iwaniec (in chronological order, [12, 13, 21, 3, 4, 5, 14]), and explaining Zhang’s innovations. These involve different types of estimates of bilinear or trilinear nature, which we present in turn. All involve estimates for exponential sums over finite fields. We therefore survey the relevant theory, separating that part depending only on one-variable character sums of Weil type (Section 4), and the much deeper one which depends on Deligne’s form of the Riemann Hypothesis (Section 6). In both cases, we present the formalism in sometimes greater generality than strictly needed, as these results are of independent interest and might be useful for other applications.

1.1. Overview of proof

We begin with a brief and informal overview of the methods used in this paper.

Important work of Fouvry and Iwaniec [12, 13] and of Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec [3, 4, 5] had succeeded, in some cases, in establishing distribution results similar to Theorem 1.1, in fact with θ\theta as large as 1/2+1/141/2+1/14, but with the restriction that the residue classes apa_{p} are obtained by reduction modulo pp of a fixed integer a≥1a\geq 1.

Following the techniques of Bombieri, Fouvry, Friedlander and Iwaniec, Zhang used the Heath-Brown identity [26] to reduce the proof of (his version of) Theorem 1.1 to the verification of three families of estimates, which he called “Type I”, “Type II”, and “Type III”. These estimates were then reduced to exponential sum estimates, using techniques such as Linnik’s dispersion method, completion of sums, and Weyl differencing. Ultimately, the exponential sum estimates were established by applications of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields, in analogy with all previous works of this type. The final part of Zhang’s argument is closely related to the study of the distribution of the ternary divisor function in arithmetic progressions by Friedlander and Iwaniec [21], and indeed the final exponential sum estimate that Zhang uses already appears in their work (this estimate was proved by Birch and Bombieri in the Appendix to [21]). An important point is that, by using techniques that are closer to some older work of Fouvry and Iwaniec [12], Zhang avoids using the spectral theory of automorphic forms, which is a key ingredient in [13] and [3], and one of the sources of the limitation to a fixed residue in these works.

Our proof of Theorem 1.1 follows the same general strategy as Zhang’s, with improvements and refinements.

First, we apply the Heath-Brown identity [26] in Section 3, with little change compared with Zhang’s argument, reducing to the “bilinear” (Types I/II) and “trilinear” (Type III) estimates.

For the Type I and Type II estimates, we follow the arguments of Zhang to reduce to the task of bounding incomplete exponential sums similar to

∑N<n≤2​Ne⁡(c1​n¯+c2​n+l¯q),\sum_{N<n\leq 2N}e\Bigl(\frac{c_{1}\bar{n}+c_{2}\overline{n+l}}{q}\Bigr),

(where e⁡(z)=e2​i​π​ze(z)=e^{2i\pi z} and x¯\bar{x} denotes the inverse of xx modulo qq) for various parameters N,c1,c2,l,qN,c_{1},c_{2},l,q. We obtain significant improvements of Zhang’s numerology at this stage, by exploiting the smooth (or at least densely divisible) nature of qq, using the qq-van der Corput AA-process of Heath-Brown [25] and Graham-Ringrose [24], combined with the Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields. Additional gains are obtained by optimizing the parameterizations of sums prior to application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In our strongest Type I estimate, we also exploit additional averaging over the modulus by means of higher-dimensional exponential sum estimates, which now do depend on the deep results of Deligne. We refer to Sections 4, 5 and 8 for details of these parts of the arguments.

Finally, for the Type III sums, Zhang’s delicate argument [52] adapts and improves the work of Friedlander and Iwaniec [21] on the ternary divisor function in arithmetic progressions. As we said, it ultimately relies on a three-variable exponential sum estimate that was proved by Birch and Bombieri in the Appendix to [21]. Here, we proceed slightly differently, inspired by the streamlined approach of Fouvry, Kowalski, and Michel [16]. Namely, in Section 7 we show how our task can be reduced to obtaining certain correlation bounds on hyper-Kloosterman sums. These bounds are established in Section 6, by fully exploiting the formalism of “trace functions” over finite fields (which relies on Deligne’s second, more general proof of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields [9]). The very general techniques presented in Section 6 are also used in the proof of the strongest Type I estimate in Section 8, and we present them in considerable detail in order to make them more accessible to analytic number theorists.

We use xx to denote a large real parameter, which one should think of as going off to infinity; in particular, we will implicitly assume that it is larger than any specified fixed constant. 2. Preliminaries

2.1. Statements of results

In this section we will give the most general statements that we prove, and in particular define the concept of “dense divisibility”, which weakens the smoothness requirement of Theorem 1.1.

Definition 2.1 (Multiple dense divisibility).

Let y≥1y\geq 1. For each natural number i≥0i\geq 0, we define a notion of ii-tuply yy-dense divisibility recursively as follows:

  • (i)

    Every natural number nn is 00-tuply yy-densely divisible.

  • (ii)

    If i≥1i\geq 1 and nn is a natural number, we say that nn is ii-tuply yy-densely divisible if, whenever j,k≥0j,k\geq 0 are natural numbers with j+k=i−1j+k=i-1, and 1≤R≤y​n1\leq R\leq yn, one can find a factorisation

    n=q​r, with ​y−1​R≤r≤Rn=qr,\quad\quad\text{ with }y^{-1}R\leq r\leq R (2.1)

    such that qq is jj-tuply yy-densely divisible and rr is kk-tuply yy-densely divisible.

We let 𝒟(i)​(y)\mathcal{D}^{({i})}({y}) denote the set of ii-tuply yy-densely divisible numbers. We abbreviate “11-tuply densely divisible” as “densely divisible”, “22-tuply densely divisible” as “doubly densely divisible”, and so forth; we also abbreviate 𝒟(1)​(y)\mathcal{D}^{({1})}({y}) as 𝒟⁡(y)\mathcal{D}({y}), and since we will often consider squarefree densely divisible integers with prime factors in an interval II, we will denote

𝒟I(j)​(y)=𝒮I∩𝒟(j)​(y).\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({j})}({y})=\mathcal{S}_{I}\cap\mathcal{D}^{({j})}({y}). (2.2)

A number of basic properties of this notion will be proved at the beginning of Section 2.3, but the intent is that we want to have integers which can always be factored, in such a way that we can control the location of the divisors. For instance, the following fact is quite easy to check: any yy-smooth integer is also ii-tuply yy-densely divisible, for any i≥0i\geq 0 (see Lemma 2.10 (iii) for details).

Definition 2.2.

For any set I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} (possibly depending on xx), let 𝒮I\mathcal{S}_{I} denote the set of all squarefree natural numbers whose prime factors lie in II. If II is also a bounded set (with the bound allowed to depend on xx), we let PIP_{I} denote the product of all the primes in II, thus in this case 𝒮I\mathcal{S}_{I} is the set of divisors of PIP_{I}.

For every fixed 0<ϖ<140<\varpi<\frac{1}{4} and 0<δ<14+ϖ0<\delta<\frac{1}{4}+\varpi and every natural number ii, we let MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] denote the following claim:

Claim 2.3 (Modified Motohashi-Pintz-Zhang estimate, MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta]).

Let I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} be a bounded set, which may vary with xx, and let Q⪻x1/2+2​ϖQ\llcurly x^{1/2+2\varpi}. If aa is an integer coprime to PIP_{I}, and A≥1A\geq 1 is fixed, then

∑q≤Qq∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)|Δ⁡(Λ​𝟏[x,2​x],a⁡(q))|≪x​log−A​x.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq Q\\ q\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\Lambda\mathbf{1}_{[x,2x]};a\ (q))|\ll x\log^{-A}x. (2.3)

We will prove the following cases of these estimates:

Theorem 2.4 (Motohashi-Pintz-Zhang type estimates).
  • (i)

    We have MPZ(4)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(4)}[\varpi,\delta] for any fixed ϖ,δ>0\varpi,\delta>0 such that 600​ϖ+180​δ<7600\varpi+180\delta<7.

  • (ii)

    We can prove MPZ(2)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(2)}[\varpi,\delta] for any fixed ϖ,δ>0\varpi,\delta>0 such that 168​ϖ+48​δ<1168\varpi+48\delta<1, without invoking any of Deligne’s results [8, 9] on the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields.

The statement MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] is easier to establish as ii increases. If true for some i≥1i\geq 1, it implies

∑q≤x1/2+2​ϖ−εq xδ-smooth, squarefree|Δ(Λ𝟏[x,2​x];a(q))|≪xlog−Ax\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq x^{1/2+2\varpi-\varepsilon}\\ q\text{ $x^{\delta}$-smooth, squarefree}\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\Lambda\mathbf{1}_{[x,2x]};a\ (q))|\ll x\log^{-A}x

for any A≥1A\geq 1 and ε>0\varepsilon>0. Using a dyadic decomposition and the Chinese Remainder Theorem, this shows that Theorem 2.4 (i) implies Theorem 1.1.

2.2. Bilinear and trilinear estimates

As explained, we will reduce Theorem 2.4 to bilinear or trilinear estimates. In order to state these precisely, we introduction some further notation.

Definition 2.5 (Coefficient sequences).

A coefficient sequence is a finitely supported sequence α:ℕ→ℝ\alpha\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} (which may depend on xx) that obeys the bounds

|α⁡(n)|≪τO⁡(1)​(n)​logO⁡(1)⁡(x)|\alpha(n)|\ll\tau^{O(1)}(n)\log^{O(1)}(x) (2.4)

for all nn (recall that τ\tau is the divisor function).

  • (i)

    A coefficient sequence α\alpha is said to be located at scale NN for some N≥1N\geq 1 if it is supported on an interval of the form [c​N,C​N][cN,CN] for some 1≪c<C≪11\ll c<C\ll 1.

  • (ii)

    A coefficient sequence α\alpha located at scale NN for some N≥1N\geq 1 is said to obey the Siegel-Walfisz theorem, or to have the Siegel-Walfisz property, if one has

    |Δ⁡(α​𝟏(⋅,r)=1,a⁡(q))|≪τ​(q​r)O⁡(1)​N​log−A​x|\Delta(\alpha\mathbf{1}_{(\cdot,r)=1};a\ (q))|\ll\tau(qr)^{O(1)}N\log^{-A}x (2.5)

    for any q,r≥1q,r\geq 1, any fixed AA, and any primitive residue class a⁡(q)a\ (q).

  • (iii)

    A coefficient sequence α\alpha is said to be shifted smooth at scale NN for some N≥1N\geq 1 if it has the form α⁡(n)=ψ⁡(n−x0N)\alpha(n)=\psi(\frac{n-x_{0}}{N}) for some smooth function ψ:ℝ→ℂ\psi\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C} supported on an interval [c,C][c,C] for some fixed 0<c<C0<c<C, and some real number x0x_{0}, with ψ\psi obeying the derivative bounds

    |ψ(j)​(x)|≪logO⁡(1)⁡x|\psi^{(j)}(x)|\ll\log^{O(1)}x (2.6)

    for all fixed j≥0j\geq 0, where the implied constant may depend on jj, and where ψ(j)\psi^{(j)} denotes the jthj^{\operatorname{th}} derivative of ψ\psi. If we can take x0=0x_{0}=0, we call α\alpha smooth at scale NN; note that such sequences are also located at scale NN.

Note that for a coefficient sequence α\alpha at scale NN, an integer q≥1q\geq 1 and a primitive residue class a⁡(q)a\ (q), we have the trivial estimate

Δ⁡(α,a⁡(q))≪Nφ⁡(q)​(log⁡x)O⁡(1).\Delta(\alpha;a\ (q))\ll\frac{N}{\varphi(q)}(\log x)^{O(1)}. (2.7)

In particular, we see that the Siegel-Walfisz property amounts to a requirement that the sequence α\alpha be uniformly equidistributed in arithmetic progressions to moduli q≪(log⁡x)Aq\ll(\log x)^{A} for any AA. In the most important arithmetic cases, it is established using the methods from the classical theory of LL-functions.

Definition 2.6 (Type I,II,III estimates).

Let 0<ϖ<1/40<\varpi<1/4, 0<δ<1/4+ϖ0<\delta<1/4+\varpi, and 0<σ<1/20<\sigma<1/2 be fixed quantities, and let i≥1i\geq 1 be a fixed natural number. We let II be an arbitrary bounded subset of ℝ\mathbb{R} and define PI=∏p∈IpP_{I}=\prod_{p\in I}p as before. Let a⁡(PI)a\ (P_{I}) be a primitive congruence class.

  • (i)

    We say that TypeI(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds if, for any II and a⁡(PI)a\ (P_{I}) as above, any quantities M,N≫1M,N\gg 1 with

    M​N≍xMN\asymp x (2.8)

    and

    x1/2−σ⪻N⪻x1/2−2​ϖ−cx^{1/2-\sigma}\llcurly N\llcurly x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} (2.9)

    for some fixed c>0c>0, any Q⪻x1/2+2​ϖQ\llcurly x^{1/2+2\varpi}, and any coefficient sequences α,β\alpha,\beta located at scales M,NM,N respectively, with β\beta having the Siegel-Walfisz property, we have

    ∑q≤Qq∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(q))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq Q\\ q\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (q))|\ll x\log^{-A}x (2.10)

    for any fixed A>0A>0. (Recall the definition (2.2) of the set 𝒟I(i)​(xδ)\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}}).)

  • (ii)

    We say that TypeII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] holds if, for any II and a⁡(PI)a\ (P_{I}) as above, any quantities M,N≫1M,N\gg 1 obeying (2.8) and

    x1/2−2​ϖ−c⪻N⪻x1/2x^{1/2-2\varpi-c}\llcurly N\llcurly x^{1/2} (2.11)

    for some sufficiently small fixed c>0c>0, any Q⪻x1/2+2​ϖQ\llcurly x^{1/2+2\varpi}, and any coefficient sequences α,β\alpha,\beta located at scales M,NM,N respectively, with β\beta having the Siegel-Walfisz property, we have (2.10) for any fixed A>0A>0.

  • (iii)

    We say that TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds if, for any II and a⁡(PI)a\ (P_{I}) as above, for any quantities M,N1,N2,N3≫1M,N_{1},N_{2},N_{3}\gg 1 which satisfy the conditions

    M​N1​N2​N3≍x\displaystyle MN_{1}N_{2}N_{3}\asymp x
    N1​N2,N1​N3,N2​N3⪼x1/2+σ\displaystyle N_{1}N_{2},N_{1}N_{3},N_{2}N_{3}\ggcurly x^{1/2+\sigma} (2.12)
    x2​σ⪻N1,N2,N3⪻x1/2−σ,\displaystyle x^{2\sigma}\llcurly N_{1},N_{2},N_{3}\llcurly x^{1/2-\sigma}, (2.13)

    for any coefficient sequences α,ψ1,ψ2,ψ3\alpha,\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3} located at scales MM, N1N_{1}, N2N_{2}, N3N_{3}, respectively, with ψ1,ψ2,ψ3\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3} smooth, and finally for any Q⪻x1/2+2​ϖQ\llcurly x^{1/2+2\varpi}, we have

    ∑q≤Qq∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)|Δ⁡(α⋆ψ1⋆ψ2⋆ψ3,a⁡(q))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq Q\\ q\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\alpha\star\psi_{1}\star\psi_{2}\star\psi_{3};a\ (q))|\\ \ll x\log^{-A}x (2.14)

    for any fixed A>0A>0.

Roughly speaking, Type I estimates control the distribution of Dirichlet convolutions α,β\alpha,\beta where α,β\alpha,\beta are rough coefficient sequences at moderately different scales, Type II estimates control the distribution of Dirichlet convolutions α,β\alpha,\beta where α,β\alpha,\beta are rough coefficient sequences at almost the same scale, and Type III estimates control the distribution of Dirichlet convolutions α⋆ψ1⋆ψ2⋆ψ3\alpha\star\psi_{1}\star\psi_{2}\star\psi_{3} where ψ1,ψ2,ψ3\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3} are smooth and α\alpha is rough but supported at a fairly small scale.

In Section 3, we will use the Heath-Brown identity to reduce MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] to a combination of TypeI(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma], TypeII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta], and TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma]:

Lemma 2.7 (Combinatorial lemma).

Let i≥1i\geq 1 be a fixed integer, and let 0<ϖ<140<\varpi<\frac{1}{4}, 0<δ<14+ϖ0<\delta<\frac{1}{4}+\varpi, and 110<σ<12\frac{1}{10}<\sigma<\frac{1}{2} be fixed quantities with σ>2​ϖ\sigma>2\varpi, such that the estimates TypeI(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma], TypeII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta], and TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] all hold. Then MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] holds.

Furthermore, if σ>1/6\sigma>1/6, then the hypothesis TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] may be omitted.

As stated earlier, this lemma is a simple consequence of the Heath-Brown identity, a dyadic decomposition (or more precisely, a finer-than-dyadic decomposition), some standard analytic number theory estimates (in particular, the Siegel-Walfisz theorem) and some elementary combinatorial arguments.

In Zhang’s work [52], the claims TypeI⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma], TypeII⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}[\varpi,\delta],TypeIII⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] are (implicitly) proven with ϖ=δ=1/1168\varpi=\delta=1/1168 and σ=1/8−8​ϖ\sigma=1/8-8\varpi. In fact, if one optimizes the numerology in his arguments, one can derive TypeI⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] whenever 44​ϖ+12​δ+8​σ<144\varpi+12\delta+8\sigma<1, TypeII⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}[\varpi,\delta] whenever 116​ϖ+20​δ<1116\varpi+20\delta<1, and TypeIII⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] whenever σ>326+3213​ϖ+213​δ\sigma>\frac{3}{26}+\frac{32}{13}\varpi+\frac{2}{13}\delta (see [45] for details). We will obtain the following improvements to these estimates, where the dependency with respect to σ\sigma is particularly important:

Theorem 2.8 (New Type I, II, III estimates).

Let ϖ,δ,σ>0\varpi,\delta,\sigma>0 be fixed quantities.

  1. (i)

    If 54​ϖ+15​δ+5​σ<154\varpi+15\delta+5\sigma<1, then TypeI(1)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(1)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds.

  2. (ii)

    If 56​ϖ+16​δ+4​σ<156\varpi+16\delta+4\sigma<1, then TypeI(2)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(2)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds.

  3. (iii)

    If 1603​ϖ+16​δ+349​σ<1\frac{160}{3}\varpi+16\delta+\frac{34}{9}\sigma<1 and 64​ϖ+18​δ+2​σ<164\varpi+18\delta+2\sigma<1, then TypeI(4)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(4)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds.

  4. (iv)

    If 68​ϖ+14​δ<168\varpi+14\delta<1, then TypeII(1)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(1)}[\varpi,\delta] holds.

  5. (v)

    If σ>118+289​ϖ+29​δ\sigma>\frac{1}{18}+\frac{28}{9}\varpi+\frac{2}{9}\delta and ϖ<1/12\varpi<1/12, then TypeIII(1)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(1)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] holds.

The proofs of the claims in (iii) and (v) require Deligne’s work on the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields, but the claims in (i), (ii) and (iv) do not.

In proving these estimates, we will rely on the following general “bilinear” form of the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem (the principle of which is due to Gallagher [22] and Motohashi [42]).

Theorem 2.9 (Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem).

Let N,M≫1N,M\gg 1 be such that N​M≍xNM\asymp x and N≥xεN\geq x^{\varepsilon} for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0. Let α,β\alpha,\beta be coefficient sequences at scale M,NM,N respectively such that β\beta has the Siegel-Walfisz property. Then for any fixed A>0A>0 there exists a fixed B>0B>0 such that

∑q≤x1/2​log−B​xsupa∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)×|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(q))|≪x​log−A​x.\sum_{q\leq x^{1/2}\log^{-B}x}\sup_{a\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (q))|\ll x\log^{-A}x.

See [3, Theorem 0] for the proof. Besides the assumption of the Siegel-Walfisz property, the other main ingredient used to establish Theorem 2.9 is the large sieve inequality for Dirichlet characters, from which the critical limitation to moduli less than x1/2x^{1/2} arises.

The Type I and Type II estimates in Theorem 2.8 will be proven in Section 5, with the exception of the more difficult Type I estimate (iii) which is proven in Section 8. The Type III estimate is established in Section 7. In practice, the estimate in Theorem 2.8(i) gives inferior results to that in Theorem 2.8(ii), but we include it here because it has a slightly simpler proof.

The proofs of these estimates involve essentially all the methods that have been developed or exploited for the study of the distribution of arithmetic functions in arithmetic progressions to large moduli, for instance the dispersion method, completion of sums, the Weyl differencing technique, and the qq-van der Corput AA process. All rely ultimately on some estimates of (incomplete) exponential sums over finite fields, either one-dimensional or higher-dimensional. These final estimates are derived from forms of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields, either in the (easier) form due to Weil [51], or in the much more general form due to Deligne [9].

2.3. Properties of dense divisibility

We present the most important properties of the notion of multiple dense divisibility, as defined in Definition 2.1. Roughly speaking, dense divisibility is a weaker form of smoothness which guaranteees a plentiful supply of divisors of the given number in any reasonable range, and multiple dense divisibility is a hereditary version of this property which also partially extends to some factors of the original number.

Lemma 2.10 (Properties of dense divisibility).

Let i≥0i\geq 0 and y≥1y\geq 1.

  • (0)

    If nn is ii-tuply yy-densely divisible, and y1≥yy_{1}\geq y, then nn is ii-tuply y1y_{1}-densely divisible. Furthermore, if 0≤j≤i0\leq j\leq i, then nn is jj-tuply yy-densely divisible.

  • (i)

    If nn is ii-tuply yy-densely divisible, and mm is a divisor of nn, then mm is ii-tuply y⁡(n/m)y(n/m)-densely divisible. Similarly, if ll is a multiple of nn, then ll is ii-tuply y⁡(l/n)y(l/n)-densely divisible.

  • (ii)

    If m,nm,n are yy-densely divisible, then [m,n][m,n] is also yy-densely divisible.

  • (iii)

    Any yy-smooth number is ii-tuply yy-densely divisible.

  • (iv)

    If nn is zz-smooth and squarefree for some z≥yz\geq y, and

    ∏p|np≤yp≥ziy,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|n\\ p\leq y\end{subarray}}p\geq\frac{z^{i}}{y}, (2.15)

    then nn is ii-tuply yy-densely divisible.

Proof.

We abbreviate “ii-tuply yy-divisible” in this proof by the shorthand “(i,y)(i,y)-d.d.”.

(0) These monotony properties are immediate from the definition.

Before we prove the other properties, we make the following remark: in checking that an integer nn is (i,y)(i,y)-d.d., it suffices to consider parameters RR with 1≤R≤n1\leq R\leq n when looking for factorizations of the form (2.1): indeed, if n<R≤y​nn<R\leq yn, the factorization n=q​rn=qr with r=nr=n and q=1q=1 satisfies the condition y−1​R≤r≤Ry^{-1}R\leq r\leq R, and r=nr=n is (j,y)(j,y)-d.d. (resp. q=1q=1 is (k,y)(k,y)-d.d.) whenever j+k=i−1j+k=i-1. We will use this reduction in (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) below.

(i) We prove the first part by induction on ii. For i=0i=0, the statement is obvious since every integer is (0,y)(0,y)-d.d. for every y≥1y\geq 1. Now assume the property holds for jj-tuply dense divisibility for j<ij<i, let nn be (i,y)(i,y)-d.d., and let m|nm\mid n be a divisor of nn. We proceed to prove that mm is (i,y​m1)(i,ym_{1})-d.d.

We write n=m​m1n=mm_{1}. Let RR be such that 1≤R≤m1\leq R\leq m, and let jj, k≥0k\geq 0 be integers with j+k=i−1j+k=i-1. Since R≤nR\leq n, and nn is (i,y)(i,y)-d.d., there exists by definition a factorization n=q​rn=qr where qq is (j,y)(j,y)-d.d., rr is (k,y)(k,y)-d.d., and y/R≤r≤yy/R\leq r\leq y. Now we write m1=n1​n1′m_{1}=n_{1}n^{\prime}_{1} were n1=(r,m1)n_{1}=(r,m_{1}) is the gcd of rr and m1m_{1}. We have then a factorization m=q1​r1m=q_{1}r_{1} where

q1=qn1′,r1=rn1,q_{1}=\frac{q}{n^{\prime}_{1}},\quad\quad r_{1}=\frac{r}{n_{1}},

and we check that this factorization satisfies the condition required for checking that mm is (i,y​m1)(i,ym_{1})-d.d. First, we have

Ry​m1≤rm1≤rn1=r1≤R,\frac{R}{ym_{1}}\leq\frac{r}{m_{1}}\leq\frac{r}{n_{1}}=r_{1}\leq R,

so the divisor r1r_{1} is well-located. Next, by induction applied to the divisor r1=r/n1r_{1}=r/n_{1} of the (k,y)(k,y)-d.d. integer rr, this integer is (k,y​n1)(k,yn_{1})-d.d., and hence by (0), it is also (k,y​m1)(k,ym_{1})-d.d. Similarly, q1q_{1} is (j,y​n1′)(j,yn^{\prime}_{1})-d.d., and hence also (j,y​m1)(j,ym_{1})-d.d. This finishes the proof that mm is (i,y​m1)(i,ym_{1})-d.d.

The second part of (i) is similar and left to the reader.

To prove (ii), recall that yy-densely divisible means (1,y)(1,y)-densely divisible. We may assume that m≤nm\leq n. Denote a=[m,n]​n−1a=[m,n]n^{-1}. Now let RR be such that 1≤R≤[m,n]1\leq R\leq[m,n]. If R≤nR\leq n, then a factorization n=q​rn=qr with R​y−1≤r≤RRy^{-1}\leq r\leq R, which exists since nn is yy-d.d., gives the factorization [m,n]=a​q​r[m,n]=aqr, which has the well-located divisor rr. If n<R≤[m,n]n<R\leq[m,n], we get

1≤na≤Ra≤n1\leq\frac{n}{a}\leq\frac{R}{a}\leq n

and therefore there exists a factorization n=q​rn=qr with R​(a​y)−1≤r≤R​a−1R(ay)^{-1}\leq r\leq Ra^{-1}. Then [m,n]=q⁡(a​r)[m,n]=q(ar) with R​y−1≤a​r≤RRy^{-1}\leq ar\leq R. Thus we see that [m,n][m,n] is yy-d.d.

We now prove (iii) by induction on ii. The case i=0i=0 is again obvious, so we assume that (iii) holds for jj-tuply dense divisibility for j<ij<i. Let nn be a yy-smooth integer, let jj, k≥0k\geq 0 satisfy j+k=i−1j+k=i-1, and let 1≤R≤n1\leq R\leq n be given. Let rr be the largest divisor of nn which is ≤R\leq R, and let q=n/rq=n/r. Since all prime divisors of nn are ≤y\leq y, we have

R​y−1≤r≤R,Ry^{-1}\leq r\leq R,

and furthermore both qq and rr are yy-smooth. By the induction hypothesis, qq is (j,y)(j,y)-d.d. and rr is (k,y)(k,y)-d.d., hence it follows that nn is (i,y)(i,y)-d.d.

We now turn to (iv). The claim is again obvious for i=0i=0. Assume then that i=1i=1. Let RR be such that 1≤R≤n1\leq R\leq n. Let

s1=∏p|np≤yp,r1=∏p|np>yp.s_{1}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\mid n\\ p\leq y\end{subarray}}p,\quad\quad r_{1}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|n\\ p>y\end{subarray}}p.

Since s1s_{1} is yy-smooth, we have r3​r2≤Rr_{3}r_{2}\leq R (since otherwise we must have r3≠1r_{3}\neq 1, hence r3r_{3} is divisible by a prime p≤yp\leq y, and r3​p−1r_{3}p^{-1} is a smaller divisor with the required property r3​p−1​r2>R​y−1r_{3}p^{-1}r_{2}>Ry^{-1}, contradicting the minimality of r3r_{3}). as desired.

Finally we consider the i>1i>1 case. We assume, by induction, that (iv) holds for integers j<ij<i. Let j,k≥0j,k\geq 0 be such that j+k=i−1j+k=i-1. By assumption, using the notation r1r_{1}, s1s_{1} as above, we have

s1≥zi​y−1=zj⋅zk⋅zy.s_{1}\geq z^{i}y^{-1}=z^{j}\cdot z^{k}\cdot\frac{z}{y}.

We can therefore write s1=n1​n2​n3s_{1}=n_{1}n_{2}n_{3} where

zj​y−1≤n1≤zj,zk​y−1≤n2≤zkz^{j}y^{-1}\leq n_{1}\leq z^{j},\quad\quad z^{k}y^{-1}\leq n_{2}\leq z^{k} (2.16)

and thus

n3≥zy.n_{3}\geq\frac{z}{y}.

Now we divide into several cases in order to find a suitable factorization of nn. Suppose first that n1≤R≤n/n2n_{1}\leq R\leq n/n_{2}. Then

1≤Rn1≤nn1​n21\leq\frac{R}{n_{1}}\leq\frac{n}{n_{1}n_{2}}

and the integer n/(n1​n2)=r1​n3n/(n_{1}n_{2})=r_{1}n_{3} satisfies the assumptions of (iv) for i=1i=1. Thus, by the previous case, we can find a factorization r1​n3=q′​r′r_{1}n_{3}=q^{\prime}r^{\prime} with y−1​Rn1≤r′≤Rn1y^{-1}\frac{R}{n_{1}}\leq r^{\prime}\leq\frac{R}{n_{1}}. We set r=n1​r′r=n_{1}r^{\prime} and q=n2​q′q=n_{2}q^{\prime}, and observe that by (2.16), rr (resp. qq) satisfies the assumption of (iv) for i=ji=j (resp. i=ki=k). By induction, the factorization n=q​rn=qr has the required property.

Next, we assume that R<n1R<n_{1}. Since n1n_{1} is yy-smooth, we can find a divisor rr of n1n_{1} such that y−1​R≤r≤Ry^{-1}R\leq r\leq R. Then q=n/rq=n/r is a multiple of n2n_{2}, and therefore it satisfies

∏p|qp≤yp≥n2≥zk​y−1.\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|q\\ p\leq y\end{subarray}}p\geq n_{2}\geq z^{k}y^{-1}.

By induction, it follows that qq is (k,y)(k,y)-d.d. Since rr is yy-smooth, qq is also (j,y)(j,y)-d.d. by (iii), and hence the factorization n=q​rn=qr is suitable in this case.

Finally, suppose that R>n/n2R>n/n_{2}, i.e., that n​R−1<n2nR^{-1}<n_{2}. We then find a factor qq of the yy-smooth integer n2n_{2} such that n​(R​y)−1≤q≤n​R−1n(Ry)^{-1}\leq q\leq nR^{-1}. Then the complementary factor r=n/qr=n/q is a multiple of n1n_{1}, and therefore it satisfies

∏p|rp≤yp≥zj​y−1,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|r\\ p\leq y\end{subarray}}p\geq z^{j}y^{-1},

so that rr is (j,y)(j,y)-d.d. by induction, and since qq is also (j,y)(j,y)-d.d. by (iii), we also have the required factorization in this case. ∎

3. Applying the Heath-Brown identity

The goal of this and the next sections is to prove the assumption MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] (Definition 2.3) for as wide a range of ϖ\varpi and δ\delta as possible, following the outline in Section 1.1. The first step, which we implement in this section, is the proof of Lemma 2.7. We follow standard arguments, particularly those in [52]. The main tool is the Heath-Brown identity, which is combined with a purely combinatorial result about finite sets of non-negative numbers. We begin with the latter statement:

Lemma 3.1.

Let 1/10<σ<1/21/10<\sigma<1/2, and let t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} be non-negative real numbers such that t1+⋯+tn=1t_{1}+\cdots+t_{n}=1. Then at least one of the following three statements holds:

  • (Type 0)

    There is a tit_{i} with ti≥1/2+σt_{i}\geq 1/2+\sigma.

  • (Type I/II)

    There is a partition {1,…,n}=S∪T\{1,\ldots,n\}=S\cup T such that

    12−σ<∑i∈Sti≤∑i∈Tti<12+σ.\frac{1}{2}-\sigma<\sum_{i\in S}t_{i}\leq\sum_{i\in T}t_{i}<\frac{1}{2}+\sigma.
  • (Type III)

    There exist distinct i,j,ki,j,k with 2​σ≤ti≤tj≤tk≤1/2−σ2\sigma\leq t_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}\leq 1/2-\sigma and

    ti+tj,ti+tk,tj+tk≥12+σ.t_{i}+t_{j},\ t_{i}+t_{k},\ t_{j}+t_{k}\geq\frac{1}{2}+\sigma. (3.1)

Furthermore, if σ>1/6\sigma>1/6, then the Type III alternative cannot occur.

Proof.

We dispose of the final claim first: if σ>1/6\sigma>1/6, then 2​σ>1/2−σ2\sigma>1/2-\sigma, and so the inequalities 2​σ≤ti≤tj≤tk≤1/2−σ2\sigma\leq t_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}\leq 1/2-\sigma of the Type III alternative are inconsistent.

Now we prove the main claim. Let σ\sigma and (t1,…,tn)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) be as in the statement. We assume that the Type 0 and Type I/II statements are false, and will deduce that the Type III statement holds.

From the failure of the Type 0 conclusion, we know that

ti<12+σt_{i}<\frac{1}{2}+\sigma (3.2)

for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. From the failure of the Type I/II conclusion, we also know that, for any S⊂{1,…,n}S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}, we have

∑i∈Sti∉(12−σ,12+σ)\sum_{i\in S}t_{i}\notin\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma,\frac{1}{2}+\sigma\Bigr)

since otherwise we would obtain the conclusion of Type I/II by taking TT to be the complement of SS, possibly after swapping the role of SS and TT.

We say that a set S⊂{1,…,n}S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\} is large if ∑i∈Sti≥12+σ\sum_{i\in S}t_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}+\sigma, and that it is small if ∑i∈Sti≤12−σ\sum_{i\in S}t_{i}\leq\frac{1}{2}-\sigma. Thus, the previous observation shows that every set S⊂{1,…,n}S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\} is either large or small, and also (from (3.2)) that singletons are small, as is the empty set. Also, it is immediate that the complement of a large set is small, and conversely (since t1+⋯+tn=1t_{1}+\cdots+t_{n}=1).

Further, we say that an element i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} is powerful if there exists a small set S⊂{1,…,n}\{i}S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\backslash\{i\} such that S∪{i}S\cup\{i\} is large, i.e., if ii can be used to turn a small set into a large set. Then we say that an element ii is powerless if it is not powerful. Thus, adding or removing a powerless element from a set SS cannot alter its smallness or largeness, and in particular, the union of a small set and a set of powerless elements is small.

We claim that there exist exactly three powerful elements. First, there must be at least two, because if PP is the set of powerless elements, then it is small, and hence its complement is large, and thus contains at least two elements, which are powerful. But picking one of these powerful ii, the set {i}∪P\{i\}\cup P is small, and therefore its complement also has at least two elements, which together with ii are three powerful elements.

Now, we observe that if ii is powerful, then ti≥2​σt_{i}\geq 2\sigma, since the gap between a large sum ∑j∈S∪{i}tj\sum_{j\in S\cup\{i\}}t_{j} and a small sum ∑j∈Stj\sum_{j\in S}t_{j} is at least 2​σ2\sigma. In particular, if i≠ji\neq j are two powerful numbers, then

ti+tj≥4​σ>12−σ,t_{i}+t_{j}\geq 4\sigma>\frac{1}{2}-\sigma,

where the second inequality holds because of the assumption σ>1/10\sigma>1/10. Thus the set {i,j}\{i,j\} is not small, and is therefore large. But then if {i,j,k,l}\{i,j,k,l\} was a set of four powerful elements, it would follow that

1=t1+⋯+tn≥(ti+tj)+(tk+tl)≥2​(12+σ)>1,1=t_{1}+\cdots+t_{n}\geq(t_{i}+t_{j})+(t_{k}+t_{l})\geq 2\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}+\sigma\Bigr)>1,

a contradiction.

Let therefore ii, jj, kk be the three powerful elements. We may order them so that ti≤tj≤tkt_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}. We have

2​σ≤ti≤tj≤tk≤12−σ2\sigma\leq t_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}\leq\frac{1}{2}-\sigma

by (3.2) and the previous argument, which also shows that {i,j}\{i,j\}, {i,k}\{i,k\} and {j,k}\{j,k\} are large, which is (3.1). ∎

Remark 3.2.

For 1/10<σ≤1/61/10<\sigma\leq 1/6, the Type III case can indeed occur, as can be seen by considering the examples (t1,t2,t3)=(2​σ,1/2−σ,1/2−σ)(t_{1},t_{2},t_{3})=(2\sigma,1/2-\sigma,1/2-\sigma). The lemma may be extended to the range 1/14<σ<1/21/14<\sigma<1/2, but at the cost of adding two additional cases (corresponding to the case of four or five powerful elements respectively):

  • (Type IV)

    There exist distinct i,j,k,li,j,k,l with 2​σ≤ti≤tj≤tk≤tl≤1/2−σ2\sigma\leq t_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}\leq t_{l}\leq 1/2-\sigma and ti+tl≥1/2+σt_{i}+t_{l}\geq 1/2+\sigma.

  • (Type V)

    There exist distinct i,j,k,l,mi,j,k,l,m with 2​σ≤ti≤tj≤tk≤tl≤tm≤1/2−σ2\sigma\leq t_{i}\leq t_{j}\leq t_{k}\leq t_{l}\leq t_{m}\leq 1/2-\sigma and ti+tj+tk≥1/2+σt_{i}+t_{j}+t_{k}\geq 1/2+\sigma.

We leave the verification of this extension to the reader. Again, for 1/14<σ≤1/101/14<\sigma\leq 1/10, the Type IV and Type V cases can indeed occur, as can be seen by considering the examples (t1,t2,t3,t4)=(2​σ,2​σ,1/2−3​σ,1/2−σ)(t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4})=(2\sigma,2\sigma,1/2-3\sigma,1/2-\sigma) and (t1,t2,t3,t4,t5)=(2​σ,2​σ,2​σ,2​σ,1−8​σ)(t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4},t_{5})=(2\sigma,2\sigma,2\sigma,2\sigma,1-8\sigma). With this extension, it is possible to extend Lemma 2.7 to the regime 1/14<σ<1/21/14<\sigma<1/2, but at the cost of requiring additional “Type IV” and “Type V” estimates as hypotheses. Unfortunately, while the methods in this paper do seem to be able to establish some Type IV estimates, they do not seem to give enough Type V estimates to make it profitable to try to take σ\sigma below 1/101/10.

To apply Lemma 3.1 to distribution theorems concerning the von Mangoldt function Λ\Lambda, we recall the Heath-Brown identity (see [26] or [30, Prop. 13.3]).

Lemma 3.3 (Heath-Brown identity).

For any K≥1K\geq 1, we have the identity

Λ=∑j=1K(−1)j−1​(Kj)​μ≤⋆j⋆𝟏⋆(j−1)⋆L\Lambda=\sum_{j=1}^{K}(-1)^{j-1}\binom{K}{j}\mu_{\leq}^{\star j}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star(j-1)}\star L (3.3)

on the interval [x,2​x][x,2x], where 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the constant function 𝟏​(n):=1\mathbf{1}(n):=1, LL is the logarithm function L⁡(n):=log⁡nL(n):=\log n, μ≤\mu_{\leq} is the truncated Möbius function

μ≤​(n):=μ⁡(n)​𝟏n≤(2​x)1/K,\mu_{\leq}(n):=\mu(n)\mathbf{1}_{n\leq(2x)^{1/K}},

and where we denote f⋆j=f⋆…⋆ff^{\star j}=f\star\ldots\star f the jj-fold Dirichlet convolution of an arithmetic function ff, i.e.,

f⋆j(n):=∑⋯∑a1⋯aj=nf(a1)⋯f(aj).f^{\star j}(n):=\mathop{\sum\cdots\sum}\limits_{a_{1}\cdots a_{j}=n}{f(a_{1})\cdots f(a_{j})}.
Proof.

Write μ=μ≤+μ>\mu=\mu_{\leq}+\mu_{>}, where μ>​(n):=μ⁡(n)​𝟏n>(2​x)1/K\mu_{>}(n):=\mu(n)\mathbf{1}_{n>(2x)^{1/K}}. Clearly the convolution

μ>⋆K⋆𝟏⋆K−1⋆L\mu_{>}^{\star K}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star K-1}\star L

vanishes on [1,2​x][1,2x]. Expanding out μ>=μ−μ≤\mu_{>}=\mu-\mu_{\leq} and using the binomial formula, we conclude that

0=∑j=0K(−1)j​(Kj)​μ⋆(K−j)⋆μ≤⋆j⋆𝟏⋆(K−1)⋆L0=\sum_{j=0}^{K}(-1)^{j}\binom{K}{j}\mu^{\star(K-j)}\star\mu_{\leq}^{\star j}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star(K-1)}\star L (3.4)

on [x,2​x][x,2x]. Since Dirichlet convolution is associative, the standard identities Λ=μ⋆L\Lambda=\mu\star L and δ=μ⋆𝟏\delta=\mu\star\mathbf{1} (where the Kronecker delta function δ⁡(n):=𝟏n=1\delta(n):=\mathbf{1}_{n=1} is the unit for Dirichlet convolution) show that the j=0j=0 term of (3.4) is

μ⋆K⋆𝟏⋆(K−1)⋆L=μ⋆L=Λ.\mu^{\star K}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star(K-1)}\star L=\mu\star L=\Lambda.

For all the other terms, we can use commutativity of Dirichlet convolution and (again) μ⋆𝟏=δ\mu\star\mathbf{1}=\delta to write

μ⋆K−j⋆μ≤⋆j⋆𝟏⋆K−1⋆L=μ≤⋆j⋆𝟏⋆(j−1)⋆L,\mu^{\star K-j}\star\mu_{\leq}^{\star j}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star K-1}\star L=\mu_{\leq}^{\star j}\star\mathbf{1}^{\star(j-1)}\star L,

so that we get (3.3). ∎

We now establish some basic properties of the arithmetic functions αk\alpha_{k} that may occur. For a subset S⊂{1​…,2​j}S\subset\{1\ldots,2j\}, we will denote by

αS:=🟊k∈S​αk\alpha_{S}:=\underset{k\in S}{\bigstar}{\alpha_{k}}

Lemma 3.4.

Let 1≤k≤2​j1\leq k\leq 2j and S⊂{1,…,2​j}S\subset\{1,\ldots,2j\}. The following facts hold:

  • (i)

    Each αk\alpha_{k} is a coefficient sequence located at scale NkN_{k}, and more generally, the convolution αS\alpha_{S} is a coefficient sequence located at scale ∏k∈SNk\prod_{k\in S}N_{k}.

  • (ii)

    If Nk≫x2​σN_{k}\gg x^{2\sigma}, then αk\alpha_{k} is smooth at scale NkN_{k}.

  • (iii)

    If Nk≫xεN_{k}\gg x^{\varepsilon} for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, then αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz property. More generally, αS\alpha_{S} satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz property if ∏k∈SNk≫xε\prod_{k\in S}N_{k}\gg x^{\varepsilon} for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0.

  • (iv)

    N1​…​N2​j≍xN_{1}\ldots N_{2j}\asymp x.

Proof.

The first part of (i) is clear from construction. For the second part of (i), we use the easily verified fact that if α,β\alpha,\beta are coefficient sequences located at scales N,MN,M respectively, then α⋆β\alpha\star\beta is a coefficient sequence located at scale N​MNM.

For (ii), we observe that since 2​σ>K−12\sigma>K^{-1}, the condition Nk≫x2​σN_{k}\gg x^{2\sigma} can only occur for k>jk>j in view of (3.9), so that αk\alpha_{k} takes the form ψNk\psi_{N_{k}} or ψNk′\psi^{\prime}_{N_{k}}, and the smoothness then follows directly from the definitions.

For (iii), the Siegel-Walfisz property for αk\alpha_{k} when k≤jk\leq j follows from the Siegel-Walfisz theorem for the Möbius function and for Dirichlet characters (see e.g. [49, Satz 4] or [30, Th. 5.29]), using summation by parts to handle the smooth cutoff, and we omit the details. For k>jk>j, αk\alpha_{k} is smooth, and the Siegel-Walfisz property for αk\alpha_{k} follows from the Poisson summation formula (and the rapid decay of the Fourier transform of smooth, compactly supported functions; compare with the arguments at the end of this section for the Type 0 case).

To handle the general case, it therefore suffices to check that if α,β\alpha,\beta are coefficient sequences located at scales N,MN,M respectively with xε≪M≪xCx^{\varepsilon}\ll M\ll x^{C} for some fixed ε,C>0\varepsilon,C>0, and β\beta satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz property, then so does α⋆β\alpha\star\beta. This is again relatively standard, but we give the proof for completeness.

By Definition 2.5, our task is to show that

|Δ⁡((α⋆β)​𝟏(⋅,q)=1,a⁡(r))|≪τ​(q​r)O⁡(1)​N​log−A​x|\Delta((\alpha\star\beta)\mathbf{1}_{(\cdot,q)=1};a\ (r))|\ll\tau(qr)^{O(1)}N\log^{-A}x

for any q,r≥1q,r\geq 1, any fixed AA, and any primitive residue class a⁡(r)a\ (r). We replace α,β\alpha,\beta by their restriction to integers coprime to q​rqr (without indicating this in the notation), which allows us to remove the constraint 𝟏(n,q)=1\mathbf{1}_{(n,q)=1}. We may also assume that r=O⁡(logA+O⁡(1)⁡x)r=O(\log^{A+O(1)}x), since the desired estimate follows from the trivial estimate (2.7) for the discrepancy otherwise.

For any integer nn, we have

∑n=a⁡(r)(α⋆β)​(n)=∑b∈(ℤ/r​ℤ)×(∑d=b⁡(r)α⁡(d))​(∑m=b¯​a​(r)β⁡(m))\sum_{n=a\ (r)}(\alpha\star\beta)(n)=\sum_{b\in(\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}\Bigl(\sum_{d=b\ (r)}\alpha(d)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{m=\bar{b}a\ (r)}\beta(m)\Bigr)

Finally, the claim (iv) follows from (3.10). ∎

We can now conclude this section by showing how the assumptions TypeI(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma], TypeII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] and TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] of Lemma 2.7 imply the estimates (3.13).

Let therefore (α1,…,α2​j)(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2j}) be given with the condition of (3.13). By Lemma 3.4(iv), we can write Nk≍xtkN_{k}\asymp x^{t_{k}} for k=1,…,2​jk=1,\ldots,2j, where the tkt_{k} are non-negative reals (not necessarily fixed) that sum to 11. By Lemma 3.1, the tit_{i} satisfy one of the three conclusions (Type 0), (Type I/II), (Type III) of that lemma. We deal with each in turn. The first case can be dealt with directly, while the others require one of the assumptions of Lemma 2.7, and we begin with these.

Suppose that we are in the Type I/II case, with the partition {1,…,2​j}=S∪T\{1,\ldots,2j\}=S\cup T given by the combinatorial lemma. We have

α1⋆⋯⋆α2​j=αS⋆αT.\alpha_{1}\star\cdots\star\alpha_{2j}=\alpha_{S}\star\alpha_{T}.

By Lemma 3.4, αS,αT\alpha_{S},\alpha_{T} are coefficient sequences located at scales NS,NTN_{S},N_{T} respectively, where

NS​NT≍x,N_{S}N_{T}\asymp x,

and (by (iii)) αS\alpha_{S} and αT\alpha_{T} satisfy the Siegel-Walfisz property. By Lemma 3.1, we also have

x1/2−σ≪NS≪NT≪x1/2+σ.x^{1/2-\sigma}\ll N_{S}\ll N_{T}\ll x^{1/2+\sigma}.

Thus, directly from Definition 2.6 and (3.6), the required estimate (3.13) follows either from the hypothesis TypeI(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] (if one has NS≤x1/2−2​ϖ−cN_{S}\leq x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} for some sufficiently small fixed c>0c>0) or from TypeII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{II}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta] (if NS>x1/2−2​ϖ−cN_{S}>x^{1/2-2\varpi-c}, for the same value of cc).

Similarly, in the Type III case, comparing Lemmas 3.4 and 3.1 with Definition 2.6 and (3.6) shows that (3.8) is a direct translation of TypeIII(i)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{III}}^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma].

It remains to prove (3.8) in the Type 0 case, and we can do this directly. In this case, there exists some k∈{1,…,2​j}k\in\{1,\ldots,2j\}, such that tk≥1/2+σ>2​σt_{k}\geq 1/2+\sigma>2\sigma. Intuitively, this means that αk\alpha_{k} is smooth (by Lemma 3.4 (ii)) and has a long support, so that it is very well-distributed in arithmetic progressions to relatively large moduli, and we can just treat the remaining αj\alpha_{j} trivially.

Precisely, we write

α1⋆…⋆α2​j=αk⋆αS\alpha_{1}\star\ldots\star\alpha_{2j}=\alpha_{k}\star\alpha_{S}

where S={1,…,2​j}\{k}S=\{1,\ldots,2j\}\backslash\{k\}. By Lemma 3.4, αk\alpha_{k} is a coefficient sequence which is smooth at a scale Nk≫x1/2+σN_{k}\gg x^{1/2+\sigma}, and αS\alpha_{S} is a coefficient sequence which is located at a scale NSN_{S} with Nk​NS≍xN_{k}N_{S}\asymp x. Δ⁡(αk⋆αS,a⁡(q))=∑m∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)×∑ℓ=m⁡(q)αS​(ℓ)​Δ​(αk,m¯​a​(q))\Delta(\alpha_{k}\star\alpha_{S};a\ (q))=\sum_{m\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}\sum_{\ell=m\ (q)}\alpha_{S}(\ell)\Delta(\alpha_{k};\bar{m}a\ (q))

If N≫x2/3N\gg x^{2/3}, then the Type 0 analysis applies again, and otherwise we may use the Type I and Type II estimates with σ>1/6\sigma>1/6.

Remark 3.6.

An inspection of the arguments shows that the interval [x,2​x][x,2x] used in Lemma 2.7 may be replaced by a more general interval [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] for any x≤x1≤x2≤2​xx\leq x_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq 2x, leading to a slight generalization of the conclusion MPZ(i)[ϖ,δ]\MPZ^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta]. By telescoping series, one may then generalize the intervals [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] further, to the range 1≤x1≤x2≤2​x1\leq x_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq 2x.

In the next sections, we will turn our attention to the task of proving distribution estimates of Type I, II and III. All three turn out to be intimately related to estimates for exponential sums over ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}, either “complete” sums over all of ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} or “incomplete” sums over suitable subsets, such as reductions modulo qq of intervals or arithmetic progressions (this link goes back to the earliest works in proving distribution estimates beyond the range of the large sieve). In the next section, we consider the basic theory of the simplest of those sums, where the essential results go back to Weil’s theory of exponential sums in one variable over finite fields. These are enough to handle basic Type I and II estimates, which we consider next. On the other hand, for Type III estimates and the most refined Type I estimates, we require the much deeper results and insights of Deligne’s second proof of the Riemann Hypothesis for algebraic varieties over finite fields.

4. One-dimensional exponential sums

The results of this section are very general and are applicable to many problems in analytic number theory. Since the account we provide might well be useful as a general reference beyond the applications to the main results of this paper, we will not use the asymptotic convention of Definition 1.2, but provide explicit estimates that can easily be quoted in other contexts. (In particular, we will sometimes introduce variables named xx in our notation.)

4.1. Preliminaries

We begin by setting up some notation and conventions. We recall from Section 1.3 that we defined eq​(a)=e2​i​π​a/qe_{q}(a)=e^{2i\pi a/q} for a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} and q≥1q\geq 1. This is a group homomorphism ℤ→ℂ×\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}, and since q​ℤ⊂ker⁡eqq\mathbb{Z}\subset\ker e_{q}, it induces naturally a homomorphism, which we also denote eqe_{q}, from ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} to ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}. In fact, for any multiple q​rqr of qq, we can also view eqe_{q} as a homomorphism ℤ/q​r​ℤ→ℂ×\mathbb{Z}/qr\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}.

It is convenient for us (and compatible with the more algebraic theory for multi-variable exponential sums discussed in Section 6) to extend further eqe_{q} to the projective line ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) by extending it by zero to the point(s) at infinity. Precisely, recall that ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) is the quotient of

Xq={(a,b)∈(ℤ/qℤ)2:a and b have no common factor},X_{q}=\{(a,b)\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{2}\colon a\text{ and }b\text{ have no common factor}\},

(where a common factor of aa and bb is a prime p|qp\mid q such that aa and bb are zero modulo pp) by the equivalence relation

(a,b)=(a​x,b​x)(a,b)=(ax,bx)

for all x∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)×x\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}. We identify ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} with a subset of ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) by sending xx to the class of (x,1)(x,1). We note that

|ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)|=q​∏p|q(1+1p),|\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})|=q\prod_{p\mid q}{\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{p}\Bigr)},

and that a point (a,b)∈ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)(a,b)\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) belongs to ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} if and only if b∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)×b\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}, in which case (a,b)=(a​b−1,1)(a,b)=(ab^{-1},1).

Thus, we can extend eqe_{q} to ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) by defining

eq​((a,b))=eq​(a​b−1)e_{q}((a,b))=e_{q}(ab^{-1})

if b∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)×b\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}, and eq​((,,,))=0e_{q}((a,b))=0 otherwise.

We have well-defined reduction maps ℙ1​(ℤ/q​r​ℤ)→ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/qr\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) for all integers r≥1r\geq 1, as well as ℙ1​(ℚ)→ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}), and we can therefore also naturally define eq​(x)e_{q}(x) for x∈ℙ1​(ℤ/q​r​ℤ)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/qr\mathbb{Z}) or for x∈ℙ1​(ℚ)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}) (for the map ℙ1​(ℚ)→ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}), we use the fact that any x∈ℙ1​(ℚ)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}) is the class of (a,b)(a,b) where aa and bb are coprime integers, so that (a⁡(q),b⁡(q))∈Xq(a\ (q),b\ (q))\in X_{q}).

We will use these extensions especially in the following context: let PP, Q∈ℤ⁡[X]Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X] be polynomials, with QQ non-zero, and consider the rational function f=PQ∈ℚ⁡(X)f=\frac{P}{Q}\in\mathbb{Q}(X). This defines a map ℙ1​(ℚ)→ℙ1​(ℚ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}), and then by reduction modulo qq, a map

f⁡(q):ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ)→ℙ1​(ℤ/q​ℤ).f\ (q)\colon\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}).

Example 4.1.

4.2. Complete exponential sums over a finite field

As is well known since early works of Davenport and Hasse in particular, the Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields (proven by Weil [51]) implies bounds with “square root cancellation” for one-dimensional exponential sums over finite fields. A special case is the following general bound:

Lemma 4.2 (One-variable exponential sums with additive characters).

Let P,Q∈ℤ⁡[X]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X] be polynomials over ℤ\mathbb{Z} in one indeterminate XX. Let pp be a prime number such that Q​(p)∈𝔽p​[X]Q\ (p)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X] is non-zero, such that there is no identity of the form

PQ​(p)=gp−g+c\frac{P}{Q}\ (p)=g^{p}-g+c (4.1)

in 𝔽p​(X)\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) for some rational function g=g⁡(X)∈𝔽p​(X)g=g(X)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) and some c∈𝔽pc\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. Then we have

|∑x∈𝔽pep​(P⁡(x)Q⁡(x))|≪p\left|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}e_{p}\left(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\right)\right|\ll\sqrt{p} (4.2)

where the implicit constant depends only on max⁡(deg⁡P,deg⁡Q)\max(\deg P,\deg Q), and this dependency is linear.

Note that, by our definitions, we have

∑x∈𝔽pep​(P⁡(x)Q⁡(x))=∑x∈𝔽pQ1​(x)≠0ep​(P1​(x)​Q1​(x)¯),\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}e_{p}\Bigl(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\Bigr)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\\ Q_{1}(x)\neq 0\end{subarray}}e_{p}(P_{1}(x)\overline{Q_{1}(x)}),

where P/Q⁡(p)=P1/Q1P/Q\ (p)=P_{1}/Q_{1} with P1P_{1}, Q1∈𝔽p​[X]Q_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X] coprime polynomials.

As key examples of Lemma 4.2, we record Weil’s bound for Kloosterman sums, namely

|∑x∈𝔽pep​(a​x+bx)|≪p\left|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}e_{p}\left(ax+\frac{b}{x}\right)\right|\ll\sqrt{p} (4.3)

when a,b∈𝔽pa,b\in\mathbb{F}_{p} are not both zero, as well as the variant

|∑x∈𝔽pep​(a​x+bx+cx+l+dx+m+ex+l+m)|≪p\left|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}e_{p}\left(ax+\frac{b}{x}+\frac{c}{x+l}+\frac{d}{x+m}+\frac{e}{x+l+m}\right)\right|\ll\sqrt{p} (4.4)

for a,b,c,d,e,l,m∈𝔽pa,b,c,d,e,l,m\in\mathbb{F}_{p} with b,c,d,e,l,m,l+mb,c,d,e,l,m,l+m non-zero. In fact, these two estimates are almost the only two cases of Lemma 4.2 that are needed in our arguments. In both cases, one can determine a suitable implied constant, e.g., the Kloosterman sum in (4.3) has modulus at most 2​p2\sqrt{p}.

We note also that the case (4.1) must be excluded, since gp​(x)−g⁡(x)+c=cg^{p}(x)-g(x)+c=c for all x∈𝔽px\in\mathbb{F}_{p}, and therefore the corresponding character sum has size equal to pp.

Proof.

This estimate follows from the Riemann Hypothesis for the algebraic curve CC over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} defined by the Artin-Schreier equation

yp−y=P⁡(x)/Q⁡(x).y^{p}-y=P(x)/Q(x).

This was first explicitly stated by Perelmuter in [44], although this was undoubtedly known to Weil; an elementary proof based on Stepanov’s method may also be found in [6]. A full proof for all curves using a minimal amount of theory of algebraic curves is found in [2]. ∎

Remark 4.3.

For our purpose of establishing some non-trivial Type I and Type II estimates for a given choice of σ\sigma (and in particular for σ\sigma slightly above 1/61/6) and for sufficiently small ϖ,δ\varpi,\delta, it is not necessary to have the full square root cancellation in (4.2), and any power savings of the form p1−cp^{1-c} for some fixed c>0c>0 would suffice (with the same dependency on PP and QQ); indeed, one obtains a non-trivial estimate for a given value of σ\sigma once one invokes the qq-van der Corput method a sufficient number of times, and once the gains from the cancellation are greater than the losses coming from completion of sums, with the latter becoming negligible in the limit ϖ,δ→0\varpi,\delta\to 0. Such a power saving (with c=1/4c=1/4) was obtained for the Kloosterman sum (4.3) by Kloosterman [34] using an elementary dilation argument (see also [41] for a generalization), but this argument does not appear to be available for estimates such as (4.4).

In order to prove parts (i), (ii) and (iv) of Theorem 2.8, we need to extend the bounds of Lemma 4.2 in two ways: to sums over ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} for qq squarefree instead of prime, and to incomplete sums over suitable subsets of ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} (the other two parts of the theorem also require exponential sum estimates, but these require the much deeper work of Deligne [9], and will be considered in Section 6).

4.3. Complete exponential sums to squarefree moduli

To extend Lemma 4.2 to squarefree moduli, we first need some preliminaries. We begin with a version of the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

Lemma 4.4 (Chinese Remainder Theorem).

If q1,q2q_{1},q_{2} are coprime natural numbers, then for any integer aa, or indeed for any a∈ℙ1​(ℚ)a\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}), we have

eq1​q2​(a)=eq1​(aq2)​eq2​(aq1).e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(a)=e_{q_{1}}\left(\frac{a}{q_{2}}\right)e_{q_{2}}\left(\frac{a}{q_{1}}\right). (4.5)

More generally, if q1,…,qkq_{1},\ldots,q_{k} are pairwise coprime natural numbers, then for any integer aa or any a∈ℙ1​(ℚ)a\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}), we have

eq1⋯qk(a)=∏i=1keqi(a∏j≠iqj).e_{q_{1}\cdots q_{k}}(a)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}e_{q_{i}}\left(\frac{a}{\prod_{j\neq i}q_{j}}\right).
Proof.

It suffices to prove the former claim for a∈ℙ1​(ℚ)a\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q}), as the latter then follows by induction.

If aa maps to a point at infinity in ℙ1​(ℤ/q1​q2​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}q_{2}\mathbb{Z}), then it must map to a point at infinity in ℙ1​(ℤ/q1​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}\mathbb{Z}) or ℙ1​(ℤ/q2​ℤ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Z}/q_{2}\mathbb{Z}), so that both sides of (4.5) are zero.

So we can assume that a∈ℤ/q1​q2​ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}q_{2}\mathbb{Z}. Let q1¯,q2¯\overline{q_{1}},\overline{q_{2}} be integers such that q1​q1¯=1​(q2)q_{1}\overline{q_{1}}=1\ (q_{2}) and q2​q2¯=1​(q1)q_{2}\overline{q_{2}}=1\ (q_{1}), respectively. Then we have q1​q1¯+q2​q2¯=1​(q1​q2)q_{1}\overline{q_{1}}+q_{2}\overline{q_{2}}=1\ (q_{1}q_{2}), and hence

eq1​q2​(a)=eq1​q2​(a⁡(q1​q1¯+q2​q2¯))=eq1​q2​(q1​q1¯​a)​eq1​q2​(q2​q2¯​a).e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(a)=e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(a(q_{1}\overline{q_{1}}+q_{2}\overline{q_{2}}))=e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(q_{1}\overline{q_{1}}a)e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(q_{2}\overline{q_{2}}a).

Since eq1​q2​(q1​q1¯​a)=eq2​(aq1)e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(q_{1}\overline{q_{1}}a)=e_{q_{2}}(\frac{a}{q_{1}}) and eq1​q2​(q2​q2¯​a)=eq1​(aq2)e_{q_{1}q_{2}}(q_{2}\overline{q_{2}}a)=e_{q_{1}}(\frac{a}{q_{2}}), the claim follows. ∎

If q∈ℤq\in\mathbb{Z} is an integer, we say that qq divides ff, and write q|fq|f, if qq divides ff in ℤ⁡[X]\mathbb{Z}[X]. We denote by (q,f)(q,f) the largest factor of qq that divides ff (i.e., the positive generator of the ideal of ℤ\mathbb{Z} consisting of integers dividing ff). Thus for instance (q,0)=q(q,0)=q. We also write f​(q)∈(ℤ/q​ℤ)​[X]f\ (q)\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})[X] for the reduction of ff modulo qq.

We need the following algebraic lemma, which can be viewed as a version of (a special case of) the fundamental theorem of calculus:

Lemma 4.5.

Let f=PQ∈ℚ⁡(X)f=\frac{P}{Q}\in\mathbb{Q}(X) with P,Q∈ℤ⁡[X]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X] coprime, and let qq be a natural number such that Q⁡(p)Q\ (p) is a non-zero polynomial for all primes p|qp\mid q (automatic if QQ is monic).

  1. (i)

    If q|f′q|f^{\prime} and all prime factors of qq are sufficiently large depending on the degrees of PP and QQ, then there exists c∈ℤ/q​ℤc\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} such that q|f−cq|f-c.

  2. (ii)

    If qq is squarefree, if Q⁡(p)Q\ (p) has degree deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q) for all p|qp\mid q and33 3 We adopt the convention deg⁡(0)=−∞\deg(0)=-\infty. deg⁡(P)<deg⁡(Q)\deg(P)<\deg(Q), and if all prime factors of qq are sufficiently large depending on the degrees of PP and QQ, then (q,f′)(q,f^{\prime}) divides (q,f)(q,f). In particular, if (q,f)=1(q,f)=1 then (q,f′)=1(q,f^{\prime})=1.

Proof.

We first prove (i). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we may assume that q=pjq=p^{j} is the power of a prime. Write f′=P1/Q1f^{\prime}=P_{1}/Q_{1} where P1P_{1} and Q1∈ℤ⁡[X]Q_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}[X] are coprime. By definition, the condition q|f′q\mid f^{\prime} implies that P1​(x)=0​(q)P_{1}(x)=0\ (q) for all x∈ℤ/q​ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}. On the other hand, since Q1​(p)Q_{1}\ (p) is non-zero in ℤ/p​ℤ​[X]\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}[X], the rational function f′​(q)f^{\prime}\ (q) is well-defined at all x∈ℤ/q​ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} except at most deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q) zeros of Q1Q_{1}, and takes the value 00 at all these ≥q−deg⁡(Q)\geq q-\deg(Q) values. If qq is large enough in terms of deg⁡(P)\deg(P) and deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q), this implies that f′​(q)=0∈ℤ/q​ℤ​[X]f^{\prime}\ (q)=0\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}[X], and therefore that f⁡(q)=cf\ (q)=c for some c∈ℤ/q​ℤc\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}, i.e., that q|f−cq\mid f-c.

Now we prove (ii). If a prime pp divides (q,f′)(q,f^{\prime}), then by (i), there exists c∈ℤ/p​ℤc\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} such that p|f−cp\mid f-c. If p∤(q,f)p\nmid(q,f), we must have c≠0c\neq 0. But then p|P−c​Qp\mid P-cQ, where P−c​Q​(p)∈ℤ/p​ℤ​[X]P-cQ\ (p)\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}[X] is (by assumption) a polynomial of degree deg⁡(Q)≥1\deg(Q)\geq 1. For p>deg⁡(Q)p>\deg(Q), this is a contradiction, so that p|(q,f)p\mid(q,f). ∎

We use this to give an estimate for complete exponential sums, which combines the bounds for Ramanujan sums with those arising from the Riemann Hypothesis for curves.

Proposition 4.6 (Ramanujan-Weil bounds).

Let qq be a squarefree natural number, and let f=PQ∈ℚ⁡(X)f=\frac{P}{Q}\in\mathbb{Q}(X), where P,Q∈ℤ⁡[X]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X] are coprime polynomials with QQ non-zero modulo pp for every p|qp\mid q, for instance QQ monic. Then we have

|∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤeq​(f⁡(n))|≤CΩ⁡(q)​q1/2​(f′,q)(f′′,q)1/2\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e_{q}(f(n))\Bigr|\leq C^{\Omega(q)}q^{1/2}\frac{(f^{\prime},q)}{(f^{\prime\prime},q)^{1/2}}

for some constant C≥1C\geq 1 depending only on deg⁡(P)\deg(P) and deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q).

Example 4.7.

(1) Let f⁡(X):=b/Xf(X):=b/X for some integer bb. We get, after changing the summation variable, a slightly weaker version of the familiar Ramanujan sum bound

|∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤe⁡(b​n)​𝟏(n,q)=1|≤(b,q)\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e(bn)\mathbf{1}_{(n,q)=1}\Bigr|\leq(b,q) (4.6)

since (q,f′)=(b,q)(q,f^{\prime})=(b,q) and (q,f′′)=c⁡(b,q)(q,f^{\prime\prime})=c(b,q) in this case for some c=1,2c=1,2.

(2) More generally, let f:=a/X+b​Xf:=a/X+bX for some integers a,ba,b. We get a weaker form of Weil’s bound for Kloosterman sums

|∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤeq​(a​n¯+b​n)​𝟏(n,q)=1|≤2Ω⁡(q)​q1/2​(a,b,q)(a,q)1/2,\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e_{q}(a\overline{n}+bn)\mathbf{1}_{(n,q)=1}\Bigr|\leq 2^{\Omega(q)}q^{1/2}\frac{(a,b,q)}{(a,q)^{1/2}},

which generalizes (4.3).

Proof.

By Lemma 4.4, we can factor the sum as a product of exponential sums over the prime divisors of qq:

∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤeq​(f⁡(n))=∏p|q∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n)(q/p)).\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e_{q}(f(n))=\prod_{p|q}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}\left(\frac{f(n)}{(q/p)}\right).

Since, for each p|qp\mid q, the constant q/pq/p is an invertible element in ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, we see that it suffices to prove the estimates

∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n))\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(f(n)) ≪p,when p|f′ (which implies p|f′′)\displaystyle\ll p,\quad\text{when $p|f^{\prime}$ (which implies $p|f^{\prime\prime}$)} (4.7)
∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n))\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(f(n)) ≪1,when p|f′′ but p∤f′\displaystyle\ll 1,\quad\text{when $p|f^{\prime\prime}$ but $p\notdivides f^{\prime}$} (4.8)
∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n))\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(f(n)) ≪p,otherwise,\displaystyle\ll\sqrt{p},\quad\text{otherwise,} (4.9)

where the implied constants, in all three cases, depend only on deg⁡(P)\deg(P) and deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q). Thus we may always assume that p|qp\mid q is large enough in terms of deg⁡(P)\deg(P) and deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q), since otherwise the result is trivial.

The first bound is clear, with implied constant equal to 11. For (4.8), since p|f′′p|f^{\prime\prime}, we conclude from Lemma 4.5 (since pp is large enough) that there exists c∈ℤ/p​ℤc\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} such that p|f′−cp|f^{\prime}-c. Since p∤f′p\notdivides f^{\prime}, we see that cc must be non-zero. Then, since f′−c=(f−c​t)′f^{\prime}-c=(f-ct)^{\prime}, another application of Lemma 4.5 shows that there exists d∈ℤ/p​ℤd\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} such that p|f−c​t−dp|f-ct-d. This implies that f⁡(n)=c​n+d⁡(p)f(n)=cn+d\ (p) whenever nn is not a pole of f⁡(p)f\ (p). The denominator QQ of ff (which is non-zero modulo pp by assumption) has at most deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q) zeroes, and therefore we see that ep​(f⁡(n))=ep​(c​n+d)e_{p}(f(n))=e_{p}(cn+d) for all but ≤deg⁡(Q)\leq\deg(Q) values of n∈ℤ/p​ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}. Thus (by orthogonality of characters) we get

|∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n))|=|∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(f⁡(n))−∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(c​n+d)|≤deg⁡(Q).\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(f(n))\Bigr|=\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(f(n))-\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}(cn+d)\Bigr|\leq\deg(Q).

Now we prove (4.9). This estimate follows immediately from Lemma 4.2, except if the reduction f~∈𝔽p​(X)\tilde{f}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) of ff modulo pp satisfies an identity

f~=gp−g+c\tilde{f}=g^{p}-g+c (4.10)

for some g∈𝔽p​(X)g\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) and c∈𝔽pc\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. We claim that, if pp is large enough, this can only happen if p|f′p\mid f^{\prime}, which contradicts the assumption of (4.9) and therefore concludes the proof.

To prove the claim, we just observe that if (4.10) holds, then any pole of gg would be a pole of f~\tilde{f} of order pp, and thus gg must be a polynomial if pp is large enough. But then (4.10) implies that f~−c\tilde{f}-c either vanishes or has degree at least pp. If pp is large enough, the latter conclusion is not possible, and thus p|f′p\mid f^{\prime}. ∎

We also need a variant of the above proposition, which is a slight refinement of an estimate appearing in the proof of [52, Proposition 11]:

Lemma 4.8.

Let d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} be squarefree integers, so that [d1,d2][d_{1},d_{2}] is squarefree, and let c1,c2,l1,l2c_{1},c_{2},l_{1},l_{2} be integers. Then there exists C≥1C\geq 1 such that

|∑n∈ℤ/[d1,d2]​ℤed1​(c1n+l1)​ed2​(c2n+l2)|≤CΩ⁡([d1,d2])​(c1,δ1)​(c2,δ2)​(d1,d2)\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/[d_{1},d_{2}]\mathbb{Z}}e_{d_{1}}\left(\frac{c_{1}}{n+l_{1}}\right)e_{d_{2}}\left(\frac{c_{2}}{n+l_{2}}\right)\Bigr|\leq C^{\Omega([d_{1},d_{2}])}(c_{1},\delta_{1})(c_{2},\delta_{2})(d_{1},d_{2})

where δi:=di/(d1,d2)\delta_{i}:=d_{i}/(d_{1},d_{2}) for i=1,2i=1,2.

Proof.

As in the proof of Proposition 4.6, we may apply Lemma 4.4 to reduce to the case where [d1,d2]=p[d_{1},d_{2}]=p is a prime number. The bound is then trivial if (c1,δ1)(c_{1},\delta_{1}), (c2,δ2)(c_{2},\delta_{2}), or (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) is equal to pp, so we may assume without loss of generality that d1=pd_{1}=p, d2=1d_{2}=1, and that c1c_{1} is coprime to pp. We then need to prove that

∑n∈ℤ/p​ℤep​(c1n+l)≪1,\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}e_{p}\left(\frac{c_{1}}{n+l}\right)\ll 1,

but this is clear since, by the change of variable m=c1/(n+l)m=c_{1}/(n+l), this sum is just a Ramanujan sum. ∎

4.4. Incomplete exponential sums

The bounds in the previous section control “complete” additive exponential sums in one variable in ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}, by which we mean sums where the variable nn ranges over all of ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}. For our applications, as well as for many others, one needs also to have good estimates for “incomplete” versions of the sums, in which the variable nn ranges over an interval, or more generally over the integers weighted by a coefficient sequence which is (shifted) smooth at some scale NN.

The most basic technique to obtain such estimates is the method of completion of sums, also called the Pólya-Vinogradov method. In essence, this is an elementary application of discrete Fourier analysis, but the importance of the results cannot be overestimated.

We begin with some facts about the discrete Fourier transform. Given a function

f:ℤ/q​ℤ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}

we define its normalized Fourier transform FTq​(f)\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f) to be the function on ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} given by

FTq​(f)​(h):=1q1/2​∑x∈ℤ/q​ℤf⁡(x)​eq​(h​x).\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f)(h):=\frac{1}{q^{1/2}}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}f(x)e_{q}(hx). (4.11)

The normalization factor 1/q1/2{1}/{q^{1/2}} is convenient because the resulting Fourier transform operator is then unitary with respect to the inner product

⟨f,g⟩:=∑x∈ℤ/q​ℤf⁡(x)​g⁡(x)¯\langle f,g\rangle:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}f(x)\overline{g(x)}

on the space of functions ℤ/q​ℤ→ℂ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}. In other words, the Plancherel formula

∑x∈ℤ/q​ℤf⁡(x)​g⁡(x)¯=∑h∈ℤ/q​ℤFTq​(f)​(h)​FTq​(g)​(h)¯\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}f(x)\overline{g(x)}=\sum_{h\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f)(h)\overline{\mathrm{FT}_{q}(g)(h)}

holds for any functions ff, g:ℤ/q​ℤ→ℂg\colon\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}. Furthermore, by the orthogonality of additive characters, we have the discrete Fourier inversion formula

FTq​(FTq​(f))​(x)=f⁡(−x)\mathrm{FT}_{q}(\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f))(x)=f(-x)

for all x∈ℤ/q​ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}.

Lemma 4.9 (Completion of sums).

Let M≥1M\geq 1 be a real number and let ψM\psi_{M} be a function on ℝ\mathbb{R} defined by

ψM​(x)=ψ​(x−x0M)\psi_{M}(x)=\psi\left(\frac{x-x_{0}}{M}\right)

where x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R} and ψ\psi is a smooth function supported on [c,C][c,C] satisfying

|ψ(j)​(x)|≪logO⁡(1)⁡M|\psi^{(j)}(x)|\ll\log^{O(1)}M

for all fixed j≥0j\geq 0, where the implied constant may depend on jj. Let q≥1q\geq 1 be an integer, and let

M′:=∑m≥1ψM​(m)≪M​(log⁡M)O⁡(1).M^{\prime}:=\sum_{m\geq 1}\psi_{M}(m)\ll M(\log M)^{O(1)}.

We have:

  1. (i)

    If f:ℤ/q​ℤ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} is a function, then

    |∑mψM​(m)​f​(m)−M′q​∑m∈ℤ/q​ℤf⁡(m)|≪q1/2​(log⁡M)O⁡(1)​suph∈ℤ/q​ℤ\{0}|FTq​(f)​(h)|.\Bigl|\sum_{m}\psi_{M}(m)f(m)-\frac{M^{\prime}}{q}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}f(m)\Bigr|\ll q^{1/2}(\log M)^{O(1)}\sup_{h\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0\}}|\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f)(h)|. (4.12)

    In particular, if M≪q​(log⁡M)O⁡(1)M\ll q(\log M)^{O(1)}, then

    |∑mψM​(m)​f​(m)|≪q1/2​(log⁡M)O⁡(1)​‖FTq​(f)‖ℓ∞​(ℤ/q​ℤ).\Bigl|\sum_{m}\psi_{M}(m)f(m)\Bigr|\ll q^{1/2}(\log M)^{O(1)}\|\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f)\|_{\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})}. (4.13)

    We also have the variant

    |∑mψM​(m)​f​(m)−M′q​∑m∈ℤ/q​ℤf⁡(m)|≪(log⁡M)O⁡(1)​Mq1/2​∑0<|h|≤q​M−1+ε|FTq​(f)​(h)|+M−A∑m∈ℤ/q​ℤ|f(m)|\Bigl|\sum_{m}\psi_{M}(m)f(m)-\frac{M^{\prime}}{q}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}f(m)\Bigr|\ll(\log M)^{O(1)}\frac{M}{q^{1/2}}\sum_{0<|h|\leq qM^{-1+\varepsilon}}|\mathrm{FT}_{q}(f)(h)|\\ +M^{-A}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}|f(m)| (4.14)

    for any fixed A>0A>0 and ε>0\varepsilon>0, where the implied constant depends on ε\varepsilon and AA.

  2. (ii)

    If II is a finite index set, and for each i∈Ii\in I, cic_{i} is a complex number and ai​(q)a_{i}\ (q) is a residue class, then for each fixed A>0A>0 and ε>0\varepsilon>0, one has

    |∑i∈Ici​∑mψM​(m)​𝟏m=ai​(q)−M′q​∑i∈Ici|≪(log⁡M)O⁡(1)​Mq​∑0<|h|≤q​M−1+ε|∑i∈Ici​eq​(ai​h)|+M−A∑i∈I|ci|,\Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}c_{i}\sum_{m}\psi_{M}(m)\mathbf{1}_{m=a_{i}\ (q)}-\frac{M^{\prime}}{q}\sum_{i\in I}c_{i}\Bigr|\ll(\log M)^{O(1)}\frac{M}{q}\sum_{0<|h|\leq qM^{-1+\varepsilon}}\Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}c_{i}e_{q}(a_{i}h)\Bigr|\\ +M^{-A}\sum_{i\in I}|c_{i}|, (4.15)

    where the implied constant depends on ε\varepsilon and AA.

Remark 4.10.

One could relax the derivative bounds on ψ\psi to |ψ(j)​(x)|≪Mεj|\psi^{(j)}(x)|\ll M^{\varepsilon_{j}} for various small fixed εj>0\varepsilon_{j}>0, at the cost of similarly worsening the various powers of log⁡M\log M in the conclusion of the lemma to small powers of MM, and assuming the εj\varepsilon_{j} small enough depending on ε\varepsilon and AA; however this variant of the lemma is a little tricky to state, and we will not have use of it here.

q1/2​FTq​(ψM,q)​(−h)=Ψ⁡(hq),q^{1/2}\mathrm{FT}_{q}(\psi_{M,q})(-h)=\Psi\Bigl(\frac{h}{q}\Bigr),

where the function Ψ\Psi is defined on ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} by
