Remark 4.11.

In Section 7, we will use a slightly refined version where the coefficients Ψ⁡(h/q)\Psi(h/q) above are not estimated trivially.

By combining this lemma with Proposition 4.6, we can obtain non-trivial bounds for incomplete exponential sums of the form

∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))

for various moduli qq, which are roughly of the shape

∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))≪q1/2+ε\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))\ll q^{1/2+\varepsilon}

when N≪qN\ll q. A number of bounds of this type were used by Zhang [52] to obtain his Type I and Type II estimates. However, it turns out that we can improve this bound for certain regimes of q,Nq,N when the modulus qq is smooth, or at least densely divisible, by using the “qq-van der Corput AA-process” of Heath-Brown [25] and Graham-Ringrose [24]. This method was introduced to handle incomplete multiplicative character sums, but it is also applicable to incomplete additive character sums. It turns out that these improved estimates lead to significant improvements in the Type I and Type II numerology over that obtained in [52].

Here is the basic estimate on incomplete one-dimensional exponential sums that we will need for the Type I and Type II estimates. Essentially the same bounds were obtained in [28, Theorem 2].

Proposition 4.12 (Incomplete additive character sums).

Let qq be a squarefree integer, and let f=PQ∈ℚ⁡(X)f=\frac{P}{Q}\in\mathbb{Q}(X) with PP, Q∈ℤ⁡[X]Q\in\mathbb{Z}[X], such that the degree of Q⁡(p)Q\ (p) is equal to deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q) for all p|qp\mid q. Assume that deg⁡(P)<deg⁡(Q)\deg(P)<\deg(Q). Set q1:=q/(f,q)q_{1}:=q/(f,q). Let further N≥1N\geq 1 be given with N≪qO⁡(1)N\ll q^{O(1)} and let ψN\psi_{N} be a function on ℝ\mathbb{R} defined by

ψN​(x)=ψ​(x−x0N)\psi_{N}(x)=\psi\left(\frac{x-x_{0}}{N}\right)

where x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R} and ψ\psi is a smooth function with compact support satisfying

|ψ(j)​(x)|≪logO⁡(1)⁡N|\psi^{(j)}(x)|\ll\log^{O(1)}N

for all fixed j≥0j\geq 0, where the implied constant may depend on jj.

  1. (i)

    (Polyá-Vinogradov + Ramanujan-Weil) We have the bound

    ∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))≪qε​(q11/2+Nq1​𝟏N≥q1​|∑n∈ℤ/q1​ℤeq1​(f⁡(n)/(f,q))|)\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))\ll q^{\varepsilon}\Bigl(q_{1}^{1/2}+\frac{N}{q_{1}}\mathbf{1}_{N\geq q_{1}}\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}\mathbb{Z}}e_{q_{1}}(f(n)/(f,q))\Bigr|\Bigr) (4.18)

    for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. In particular, lifting the ℤ/q1​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}\mathbb{Z} sum to a ℤ/q​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} sum, we have

    ∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))≪qε​(q1/2+Nq​|∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤeq​(f⁡(n))|)\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))\ll q^{\varepsilon}\Bigl(q^{1/2}+\frac{N}{q}\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e_{q}(f(n))\Bigr|\Bigr) (4.19)
  2. (ii)

    (one van der Corput + Ramanujan-Weil) If q=r​sq=rs, then we have the additional bound

    ∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))≪qε​((N1/2​r11/2+N1/2​s11/4)+Nq1​𝟏N≥q1​|∑n∈ℤ/q1​ℤeq1​(f⁡(n)/(f,q))|)\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))\ll q^{\varepsilon}\left(\Bigl(N^{1/2}r_{1}^{1/2}+N^{1/2}s_{1}^{1/4}\Bigr)+\frac{N}{q_{1}}\mathbf{1}_{N\geq q_{1}}\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q_{1}\mathbb{Z}}e_{q_{1}}(f(n)/(f,q))\Bigr|\right) (4.20)

    for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, where r1:=(r,q1)r_{1}:=(r,q_{1}) and s1:=(s,q1)s_{1}:=(s,q_{1}). In particular, we have

    ∑nψN​(n)​eq​(f⁡(n))≪qε​((N1/2​r1/2+N1/2​s1/4)+Nq​|∑n∈ℤ/q​ℤeq​(f⁡(n))|).\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)e_{q}(f(n))\ll q^{\varepsilon}\left(\Bigl(N^{1/2}r^{1/2}+N^{1/2}s^{1/4}\Bigr)+\frac{N}{q}\Bigl|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}e_{q}(f(n))\Bigr|\right). (4.21)

In all cases the implied constants depend on ε\varepsilon, deg⁡(P)\deg(P), deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q) and the implied constants in the estimates for the derivatives of ψ\psi.

Remark 4.13.

The estimates obtained by completion of sums are usually inefficient in the regime M=o⁡(q)M=o(q), and they become trivial for M≪q1/2M\ll q^{1/2}. For instance, when ff is bounded in magnitude by 11, the trivial bound for the right-hand side of (4.13) is qq, whereas the trivial bound for the left-hand side is of size about MM, which means that one needs a cancellation at least by a factor q/Mq/M in the right-hand side to even recover the trivial bound. This becomes a prohibitive restriction if this factor is larger than M\sqrt{M}. In this paper, this inefficiency is a major source of loss in our final exponents (the other main source being our frequent reliance on the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as each invocation of this inequality tends to halve all gains in exponents arising from application of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields). It would thus be of considerable interest to find stronger estimates for incomplete exponential sums. But the only different (general) method we are aware of is the recent “sliding sum method” of Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel [18], which however only improves on the completion technique when MM is very close to q1/2q^{1/2}, and does not give stronger bounds than Lemma 4.9 and Proposition 4.12 in most ranges of interest. (Note however that uniformity of estimates is often even more crucial to obtaining good results, and for this purpose, the completion techniques are indeed quite efficient.)

Proof.

We begin with some technical reductions. First of all, we may assume that qq has no prime factor smaller than any fixed BB depending on deg⁡(P)\deg(P) and deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q), as the general case then follows by factoring out a bounded factor from qq and splitting the summation over nn into a bounded number of pieces.

Second, we also observe that, in all cases, we may replace ff by f/(f,q)f/(f,q) and qq by q1q_{1} and (in the case when q=r​sq=rs) rr by r1r_{1} and ss by s1s_{1}, since if we write q=q1​q2q=q_{1}q_{2} we have

eq​(f⁡(n))=eq1​(P⁡(n)q2​Q​(n)).e_{q}(f(n))=e_{q_{1}}\Bigl(\frac{P(n)}{q_{2}Q(n)}\Bigr).

Thus we can reduce to a situation where (f,q)=1(f,q)=1, so q=q1q=q_{1}, r=r1r=r_{1} and s=s1s=s_{1}. We now establish (4.18). We apply (4.14), and put the “main term” with h=0h=0 in the right-hand side, to get

If N<qN<q, Proposition 4.6 applied for all hh gives

In our particular application, we only need a special case of the above proposition. This is a strengthening of [52, Lemma 11], and it shows how an assumption of dense divisibility of a modulus may be exploited in estimates for exponential sums.

5. Type I and Type II estimates

Using the estimates of the previous section, we can now prove the Type I and Type II results of Theorem 2.8, with the exception of part (iii) of that theorem in which we only make a preliminary reduction for now. The rest of the proof of that part, which depends on the concepts and results of Section 6, will be found in Section 8.

We recall the statements (see Definition 2.6).

Theorem 5.1 (New Type I and Type II estimates).

Let ϖ,δ,σ>0\varpi,\delta,\sigma>0 be fixed quantities, let II be a bounded subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}, let i≥1i\geq 1 be fixed, let a⁡(PI)a\ (P_{I}) be a primitive congruence class, and let M,N≫1M,N\gg 1 be quantities with

M​N≍xMN\asymp x (5.1)

and

for any fixed A>0A>0, provided that one of the following hypotheses holds:

  1. (i)

    i=1i=1, 54​ϖ+15​δ+5​σ<154\varpi+15\delta+5\sigma<1, and N⪻x1/2−2​ϖ−cN\llcurly x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} for some fixed c>0c>0.

  3. (iii)

    i=4i=4, 1603​ϖ+16​δ+349​σ<1\frac{160}{3}\varpi+16\delta+\frac{34}{9}\sigma<1, 64​ϖ+18​δ+2​σ<164\varpi+18\delta+2\sigma<1, and N⪻x1/2−2​ϖ−cN\llcurly x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} for some fixed c>0c>0.

    i=1i=1, 68​ϖ+14​δ<168\varpi+14\delta<1, and N⪼x1/2−2​ϖ−cN\ggcurly x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} for some sufficiently small fixed c>0c>0.

The proof of the case (iii) uses the general form of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields [9], but the proofs of (i), (ii), (iv) only need the Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields.

Before we begin the rigorous proof of Theorem 5.1, we give an informal sketch of our strategy of proof for these estimates, which is closely modeled on the arguments of Zhang [52]. The basic idea is to reduce the estimate (5.3) to a certain exponential sum estimate, of the type found in Corollary 4.16 (and, for the estimate (iii), in Corollary 6.24 of the next section). The main tools for these reductions are completion of sums (Lemma 4.9), the triangle inequality, and many techniques related to the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (viewed in a broad sense), for instance Vinogradov’s bilinear form method, the qq-van der Corput AA-process, the method of Weyl differencing, or the dispersion method of Linnik.

5.1. Bilinear form estimates

We begin with a short discussion of typical instances of applications of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (some examples already appeared in previous sections). We want to estimate a sum

∑s∈Scs\sum_{s\in S}c_{s}

of (typically) complex numbers csc_{s} indexed by some finite set SS of large size. Suppose we can parameterize SS (possibly with repetition) by a non-trivial product set A×BA\times B, i.e., by a product where neither factor is too small, or otherwise prove an inequality

|∑s∈Scs|≤|∑a∈A∑b∈Bαa​βb​ka,b|\Bigl|\sum_{s\in S}c_{s}\Bigr|\leq\Bigl|\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{b\in B}\alpha_{a}\beta_{b}k_{a,b}\Bigr|

for certain coefficients αa\alpha_{a}, βb\beta_{b} and ka,bk_{a,b}. The crucial insight is that one can often derive non-trivial estimates for an expression of this type with little knowledge of the coefficients αa\alpha_{a}, βb\beta_{b}, by exploiting the bilinear structure and studying the coefficients ka,bk_{a,b}.

Precisely, one can apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to bound the right-hand side by

(∑a∈A|αa|2)1/2​(∑a∈A|∑b∈Bβb​ka,b|2)1/2.\left(\sum_{a\in A}|\alpha_{a}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{a\in A}\left|\sum_{b\in B}\beta_{b}k_{a,b}\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2}.

The first factor in the above expression is usually easy to estimate, and the second factor can be expanded as

|∑b,b′∈Bβb​βb′¯​C​(b,b′)|1/2,C⁡(b,b′)=∑a∈Aka,b​ka,b′¯.\Bigl|\sum_{b,b^{\prime}\in B}\beta_{b}\overline{\beta_{b^{\prime}}}C(b,b^{\prime})\Bigr|^{1/2},\quad\quad C(b,b^{\prime})=\sum_{a\in A}k_{a,b}\overline{k_{a,b^{\prime}}}.

One can then distinguish between the diagonal contribution defined by b=b′b=b^{\prime} and the off-diagonal contribution where b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime}. The contribution of the former is

∑b∈B∑a∈A|βb|2​|ka,b|2\sum_{b\in B}\sum_{a\in A}|\beta_{b}|^{2}|k_{a,b}|^{2}

which is (usually) not small, since there cannot be cancellation between these non-negative terms. It may however be estimated satisfactorily, provided BB is large enough for the diagonal {(b,b):b∈B}\{(b,b):b\in B\} to be a “small” subset of the square B×BB\times B. (In practice, there might be a larger subset of B×BB\times B than the diagonal where the coefficient C⁡(b,b′)C(b,b^{\prime}) is not small, and that is then incorporated in the diagonal; in this paper, where bb and b′b^{\prime} are integers, it is the size of a gcd (b−b′,q)(b-b^{\prime},q) that will dictate which terms can be considered diagonal).

On the other hand, the individual off-diagonal terms C⁡(b,b′)C(b,b^{\prime}) can be expected to exhibit cancellation that makes them individually small. In order for the sum over b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime} to remain of manageable size, one needs BB to remain not too large. In order to balance the two contributions, it turns out to be extremely useful to have a flexible family of parameterizations (a,b)↦s(a,b)\mapsto s of SS by product sets A×BA\times B, so that one can find a parameterization for which the set BB is close to the optimum size arising from various estimates of the diagonal and non-diagonal parts. This idea of flexibility is a key idea at least since Iwaniec’s discovery [29] of the bilinear form of the error term in the linear sieve.

One of the key ideas in Zhang’s paper [52] is that if one is summing over smooth moduli, then such a flexible range of factorizations exists; to put it another way, the restriction to smooth moduli is essentially a “well-factorable” weight in the sense of Iwaniec. In this paper, we isolated the key property of smooth moduli needed for such arguments, namely the property of dense divisibility. The general strategy is thus to keep exploiting the smoothness or dense divisibility of the moduli to split the sums over such moduli into a “well-factorable” form to which the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality may be profitably applied. (Such a strategy was already used to optimize the use of the qq-van der Corput AA-process in Corollary 4.16.)

5.2. Sketch of proofs

We now give a more detailed, but still very informal, sketch of the proof of Theorem 5.1, omitting some steps and some terms for sake of exposition (e.g., smooth cutoffs are not mentioned). For simplicity we will pretend that the quantities ϖ,δ\varpi,\delta are negligible, although the quantity σ\sigma will still be of a significant size (note from Lemma 2.7 that we will eventually need to take σ\sigma to be at least 1/101/10). The first step is to exploit the dense divisibility of the modulus dd to factor it as d=q​rd=qr, with q,rq,r located at certain scales Q,RQ,R which we will specify later; with ϖ\varpi negligible, we expect Q​RQR to be approximately equal to x1/2x^{1/2} but a bit larger. Our task is then to obtain a non-trivial bound on the quantity

∑q≍Q∑r≍R|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(q​r))|,\sum_{q\asymp Q}\sum_{r\asymp R}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (qr))|,

or equivalently to obtain a non-trivial bound on

∑q≍Q∑r≍Rcq,r​Δ​(α⋆β,a⁡(q​r))\sum_{q\asymp Q}\sum_{r\asymp R}c_{q,r}\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (qr))

for an arbitrary bounded sequence cq,rc_{q,r}. We suppress here, and later, some additional information on the moduli q,rq,r, e.g. that they are squarefree and coprime, to simplify this informal exposition. For similar reasons we are being vague on what a “non-trivial bound” means, but roughly speaking, it should improve upon the “trivial bound” by a factor of log−A⁡x\log^{-A}x where AA is very large (or arbitrarily large).

If we insert the definition (1.1), and denote generically by EMT\mathrm{EMT} the contribution of the second term in that definition (which is the “expected main term”), we see that we need a non-trivial bound on the quantity

∑q≍Q∑r≍Rcq,r​∑n=a⁡(q​r)α⋆β⁡(n)−EMT.\sum_{q\asymp Q}\sum_{r\asymp R}c_{q,r}\sum_{n=a\ (qr)}\alpha\star\beta(n)-\mathrm{EMT}.

For simplicity, we will handle the rr averaging trivially, and thus seek to control the sum

∑q≍Qcq,r​∑n=a⁡(q​r)α⋆β⁡(n)−EMT\sum_{q\asymp Q}c_{q,r}\sum_{n=a\ (qr)}\alpha\star\beta(n)-\mathrm{EMT}

for a single r≍Rr\asymp R. We rearrange this as

∑m≍Mα⁡(m)​∑q≍Qcq,r​∑n≍Nn​m=a⁡(q​r)β⁡(n)−EMT.\sum_{m\asymp M}\alpha(m)\sum_{q\asymp Q}c_{q,r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\asymp N\\ nm=a\ (qr)\end{subarray}}\beta(n)-\mathrm{EMT}.

Note that for fixed mm coprime with qq, the number of pairs (q,n)(q,n) with q≍Qq\asymp Q, n≍Nn\asymp N, and n​m=a⁡(q​r)nm=a\ (qr) is expected to be about Q​NQ​R=NR\frac{QN}{QR}=\frac{N}{R}. Thus, if we choose RR to be a little bit less than NN, e.g. R=x−ε​NR=x^{-\varepsilon}N, then the number of pairs (q,n)(q,n) associated to a given value of mm is expected to be non-trivial. This opens up the possibility of using the dispersion method of Linnik [37], as the diagonal contribution in that method is expected to be negligible. Accordingly, we apply Cauchy-Schwarz in the variable mm, eliminating the rough coefficient sequence α\alpha, and end up with the task of controlling an expression of the shape

∑m≍M|∑q≍Qcq,r​∑n≍Nn​m=a⁡(q​r)β⁡(n)−EMT|2.\sum_{m\asymp M}\Bigl|\sum_{q\asymp Q}c_{q,r}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\asymp N\\ nm=a\ (qr)\end{subarray}}\beta(n)-\mathrm{EMT}\Bigr|^{2}.

Opening the square as sketched above, this is equal to

∑q1,q2≍Qcq1,r​cq2,r¯​∑∑n1,n2≍N⁡β⁡(n1)​β⁡(n2)¯​(∑m≍Mn1​m=a⁡(q1​r)n2​m=a⁡(q2​r)1−EMT).\sum_{q_{1},q_{2}\asymp Q}c_{q_{1},r}\overline{c_{q_{2},r}}\mathop{\sum\sum}\limits_{n_{1},n_{2}\asymp N}\beta(n_{1})\overline{\beta(n_{2})}\Bigl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\asymp M\\ n_{1}m=a\ (q_{1}r)\\ n_{2}m=a\ (q_{2}r)\end{subarray}}1-\mathrm{EMT}\Bigr).

Note that, since a⁡(q​r)a\ (qr) is a primitive residue class, the constraints n1​m=a⁡(q1​r),n2​m=a⁡(q2​r)n_{1}m=a\ (q_{1}r),n_{2}m=a\ (q_{2}r) imply n1=n2​(r)n_{1}=n_{2}\ (r). Thus we can write n2=n1+ℓ​rn_{2}=n_{1}+\ell r for some ℓ=O⁡(N/R)\ell=O(N/R), which will be rather small (compare with the method of Weyl differencing).

For simplicity, we consider only44 4 Actually, for technical reasons, in the rigorous argument we will dispose of the ℓ=0\ell=0 contribution by a different method, so the discussion here should be viewed as an oversimplification. the case ℓ=0\ell=0 here. We are thus led to the task of controlling sums such as

∑q1,q2≍Qcq1,r​cq2,r¯​∑n≍Nβ⁡(n)​β⁡(n)¯​(∑m≍Mn​m=a⁡(q1​r)n​m=a⁡(q2​r)1−EMT).\sum_{q_{1},q_{2}\asymp Q}c_{q_{1},r}\overline{c_{q_{2},r}}\sum_{n\asymp N}\beta(n)\overline{\beta(n)}\Bigl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\asymp M\\ nm=a\ (q_{1}r)\\ nm=a\ (q_{2}r)\end{subarray}}1-\mathrm{EMT}\Bigr). (5.4)

It turns out (using a technical trick of Zhang which we will describe below) that we can ensure that the moduli q1,q2q_{1},q_{2} appearing here are usually coprime, in the sense that the contribution of the non-coprime pairs q1,q2q_{1},q_{2} are negligible. Assuming this, we can use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to combine the two constraints n​m=a⁡(q1​r)nm=a\ (q_{1}r), n​m=a⁡(q2​r)nm=a\ (q_{2}r) into a single constraint n​m=a⁡(q1​q2​r)nm=a\ (q_{1}q_{2}r) on mm. Now, we note that if RR is slightly less than NN, then (since M​NMN is close to xx, and Q​RQR is close to x1/2x^{1/2}) the modulus q1​q2​rq_{1}q_{2}r is comparable to MM. This means that the inner sum

∑m≍Mn​m=a⁡(q1​q2​r)1−EMT\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\asymp M\\ nm=a\ (q_{1}q_{2}r)\end{subarray}}1-\mathrm{EMT}

is essentially a complete sum, and can therefore be very efficiently handled by Lemma 4.9. This transforms (5.4) into expressions such as

∑0<|h|≤Hch​∑q1,q2≍Qcq1,r​cq2,r¯​∑n≍Nβ⁡(n)​β⁡(n)¯​eq1​q2​r​(a​hn),\sum_{0<|h|\leq H}c_{h}\sum_{q_{1},q_{2}\asymp Q}c_{q_{1},r}\overline{c_{q_{2},r}}\sum_{n\asymp N}\beta(n)\overline{\beta(n)}e_{q_{1}q_{2}r}\left(\frac{ah}{n}\right),

where H≈Q2​RMH\approx\frac{Q^{2}R}{M} is a fairly small quantity, and the coefficients chc_{h} are bounded. At this point, the contribution of the zero frequency h=0h=0 has cancelled out with the expected main term EMT\mathrm{EMT} (up to negligible error).

This expression involves the essentially unknown (but bounded) coefficients cq1,rc_{q_{1},r}, cq2,rc_{q_{2},r}, β⁡(n)\beta(n), and as before, we can not do much more than eliminate them using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. This can be done in several ways here, depending on which variables are taken “outside” of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. For instance, if we take nn to eliminate the β⁡(n)​β⁡(n)¯\beta(n)\overline{\beta(n)} term, one is led, after expanding the square and exchanging the sum in the second factor of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, to expressions such as

∑0<|h1|,|h2|≤H∑∑q1,q2,s1,s2≍Q⁡|∑n≍Neq1​q2​r​(a​h1n)​es1​s2​r​(−a​h2n)|.\sum_{0<|h_{1}|,|h_{2}|\leq H}\mathop{\sum\sum}\limits_{q_{1},q_{2},s_{1},s_{2}\asymp Q}\left|\sum_{n\asymp N}e_{q_{1}q_{2}r}\left(\frac{ah_{1}}{n}\right)e_{s_{1}s_{2}r}\left(-\frac{ah_{2}}{n}\right)\right|.

The sum over nn has length NN close to the modulus [q1​q2​r,s1​s2​r]≈Q4​R[q_{1}q_{2}r,s_{1}s_{2}r]\approx Q^{4}R, and therefore can be estimated non-trivially using Corollary 4.16. As we will see, this arrangement of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is sufficient to establish the Type II estimate (iv).

The Type I estimates are obtained by a slightly different application of Cauchy-Schwarz. Indeed, note for instance that as the parameter σ\sigma (which occurs in the Type I condition, but not in Type II) gets larger, the length NN in the sum may become smaller in comparison to the modulus q1​q2​s1​s2​rq_{1}q_{2}s_{1}s_{2}r in the exponential sum

∑n≍Neq1​q2​r​(a​h1n)​es1​s2​r​(−a​h2n),\sum_{n\asymp N}e_{q_{1}q_{2}r}\left(\frac{ah_{1}}{n}\right)e_{s_{1}s_{2}r}\left(-\frac{ah_{2}}{n}\right),

and this necessitates more advanced exponential sum estimates to recover non-trivial cancellation. Here, the qq-van der Corput AA-method enlarges the range of parameters for which we can prove that such a cancellation occurs. This is one of the main reasons why our Type I estimates improve on those in [52]. (The other main reason is that we will adjust the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to lower the modulus in the exponential sum to be significantly smaller than q1​q2​s1​s2​r≍Q4​Rq_{1}q_{2}s_{1}s_{2}r\asymp Q^{4}R, while still keeping both the diagonal and off-diagonal components of the Cauchy-Schwarz estimate under control.)

5.3. Reduction to exponential sums

We now turn to the details of the above strategy. We begin with the preliminary manipulations (mostly following [52]) to reduce the estimate (5.3) to a certain exponential sum estimate. This reduction can be done simultaneously in the four cases (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), but the verification of the exponential sum estimate requires a different argument in each of the four cases.

In the remainder of this section ϖ,δ,σ,I,i,a,M,N,α,β\varpi,\delta,\sigma,I,i,a,M,N,\alpha,\beta are as in Theorem 5.1. First of all, since β\beta satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz property, the Bombieri-Vinogradov Theorem 2.9 implies

∑d≤x1/2​log−B​x|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(d))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{d\leq x^{1/2}\log^{-B}x}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (d))|\ll x\log^{-A}x (5.5)

for any fixed A>0A>0 and some BB depending on AA. From this and dyadic decomposition, we conclude that to prove (5.3), it suffices to establish the estimate

∑d∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)∩[D,2​D]|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(d))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\cap[D,2D]}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (d))|\ll x\log^{-A}x

for any fixed A>0A>0, and for all DD such that

x1/2⪻D⪻x1/2+2​ϖx^{1/2}\llcurly D\llcurly x^{1/2+2\varpi} (5.6)

We now fix one such DD. In the spirit of [52], we first restrict dd to moduli which do not have too many small prime factors. Precisely, let

D0:=exp⁡(log1/3⁡x),D_{0}:=\exp(\log^{1/3}x), (5.7)

and let ℰ⁡(D)\mathcal{E}(D) be the set of d∈[D,2​D]d\in[D,2D] such that

∏p|dp≤D0p>exp⁡(log2/3⁡x).\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|d\\ p\leq D_{0}\end{subarray}}p>\exp(\log^{2/3}x). (5.8)

We have (cf. [11, lemme 4]):

Lemma 5.2.

For any fixed A>0A>0, and DD obeying (5.6), we have

|ℰ⁡(D)|≪D​log−A​x.|\mathcal{E}(D)|\ll D\log^{-A}x.
Proof.

If d≥1d\geq 1 satisfies (5.8), then

∏p|dp≤D0p>exp⁡(log2/3⁡x)=D0log1/3⁡x.\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p|d\\ p\leq D_{0}\end{subarray}}p>\exp(\log^{2/3}x)=D_{0}^{\log^{1/3}x}.

In particular, dd has at least log1/3⁡x\log^{1/3}x prime factors, and therefore

τ⁡(d)≥2log1/3⁡x.\tau(d)\geq 2^{\log^{1/3}x}.

On the other hand, we have

∑D≤d≤2​Dτ⁡(d)≥κ1≤1κ​∑D≤d≤2​Dτ⁡(d)≪Dκ​log⁡x\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\leq d\leq 2D\\ \tau(d)\geq\kappa\end{subarray}}1\leq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{D\leq d\leq 2D}{\tau(d)}\ll\frac{D}{\kappa}\log x

for any κ>0\kappa>0 by the standard bound

(see (1.3)), and the result follows. ∎

This allows us to dispose of these exceptional moduli:

Corollary 5.3.

We have

∑d∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)d∈ℰ⁡(D)|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(d))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\\ d\in\mathcal{E}(D)\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (d))|\ll x\log^{-A}x

for any fixed A>0A>0.

Proof.

From (1.4) we derive the trivial bound

|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(d))|≪x​D−1​τ​(d)O⁡(1)​logO⁡(1)​x,|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (d))|\ll xD^{-1}\tau(d)^{O(1)}\log^{O(1)}x,

for every d≍Dd\asymp D, and hence the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives

It therefore suffices to show that

∑d∈𝒟I(i)​(xδ)d∈[D,2​D]\ℰ⁡(D)|Δ⁡(α⋆β,a⁡(d))|≪x​log−A​x\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({i})}({x^{\delta}})\\ d\in[D,2D]\backslash\mathcal{E}(D)\end{subarray}}|\Delta(\alpha\star\beta;a\ (d))|\ll x\log^{-A}x (5.9)

for any fixed A>0A>0.

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be a small fixed quantity to be chosen later. From (5.2) and (5.6) we have

1≤x−3​ε​N≤D1\leq x^{-3\varepsilon}N\leq D

By Lemma 2.10(0), (i), we have

q∈𝒟(j)​(s​xδ)=𝒟(j)​(xδ+o⁡(1)),r∈𝒟(k)​(s​xδ)=𝒟(k)​(xδ+o⁡(1)).q\in\mathcal{D}^{({j})}({sx^{\delta}})=\mathcal{D}^{({j})}({x^{\delta+o(1)}}),\quad\quad r\in\mathcal{D}^{({k})}({sx^{\delta}})=\mathcal{D}^{({k})}({x^{\delta+o(1)}}).

In particular, q∈𝒟J(j)​(xδ+o⁡(1))q\in\mathcal{D}_{{J}}^{({j})}({x^{\delta+o(1)}}) where J:=I∩(D0,+∞)J:=I\cap(D_{0},+\infty). As i≥1i\geq 1, we also have q​r=d∈𝒟I​(xδ)=𝒟I(1)​(xδ)qr=d\in\mathcal{D}_{{I}}({x^{\delta}})=\mathcal{D}_{{I}}^{({1})}({x^{\delta}}).

By excluding the small primes from q1,q2q_{1},q_{2}, this will ensure that q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} will almost always be coprime, which will make things much simpler.

and

for any summands Aq,ArA_{q},A_{r}.

We have

for any smooth coefficient sequence ψM\psi_{M} at scale MM such that ψM​(m)≥1\psi_{M}(m)\geq 1 for mm in the support of β\beta. This means in particular that it is enough to prove the estimate

Let Σ\Sigma denote the left-hand side of (5.19). Expanding the square, we find

Remark 5.9.

As before, one should consider the q0=1q_{0}=1 case as the main case, so that the technical factors of q0q_{0}, (ℓ,q0)(\ell,q_{0}), and C⁡(n)C(n) should be ignored at a first reading; in practice, we will usually (though not always) end up discarding several powers of q0q_{0} in the denominator in the final bounds for the q0>1q_{0}>1 case. The trivial bound for Υℓ,r​(b1,b2,q0)\Upsilon_{\ell,r}(b_{1},b_{2};q_{0}) is about (Q/q0)2​N​H(Q/q_{0})^{2}NH with H=xε​R​Q2​M−1​q0−1H=x^{\varepsilon}RQ^{2}M^{-1}q_{0}^{-1}. Thus one needs to gain about HH over the trivial bound. As observed previously, HH is quite small, and even a modestly non-trivial exponential sum estimate can suffice for this purpose (after using Cauchy-Schwarz to eliminate factors such as β⁡(n)​β⁡(n+ℓ​r)¯\beta(n)\overline{\beta(n+\ell r)}).

It remains to establish Theorem 5.8 in the four cases indicated. We will do this for (i), (ii), (iv) below, and defer the proof of (iii) to Section 8. In all four cases, one uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to eliminate non-smooth factors such as β⁡(n)\beta(n) and β⁡(n+ℓ​r)\beta(n+\ell r), and reduces matters to incomplete exponential sum estimates. In the cases (i), (ii), (iv) treated below, the one-dimensional exponential sum estimates from Section 4.4 suffice; for the final case (iii), a multidimensional exponential sum estimate is involved, and we will prove it using Deligne’s formalism of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields, which we survey in Section 6.

Remark 5.11.

By replacing the lower bound N⪼x1/2−2​ϖ−cN\ggcurly x^{1/2-2\varpi-c} with the lower bound N⪼x1/2−σN\ggcurly x^{1/2-\sigma}, the above argument also yields the estimate TypeI(1)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(1)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] whenever 48​ϖ+14​δ+10​σ<148\varpi+14\delta+10\sigma<1. However, as this constraint does not allow σ\sigma to exceed 1/101/10, one cannot use this estimate as a substitute for Theorem 2.8(ii) or Theorem 2.8(iii). If one uses the first estimate of Corollary 4.16 in place of the second, one can instead obtain TypeI(1)⁡[ϖ,δ,σ]\operatorname{Type}_{\operatorname{I}}^{(1)}[\varpi,\delta,\sigma] for the range 56​ϖ+16​δ+6​σ<156\varpi+16\delta+6\sigma<1, which now does permit σ\sigma to exceed 1/101/10, and thus gives some version of Zhang’s theorem after combining with a Type III estimate. However, σ\sigma still does not exceed 1/61/6, and so one cannot dispense with the Type III component of the argument entirely with this Type I estimate. By using a second application of qq-van der Corput, though (i.e. using the l=3l=3 case of Proposition 4.12 rather than the l=2l=2 case), it is possible to raise σ\sigma above 1/61/6, assuming sufficient amounts of dense divisibility; we leave the details to the interested reader. However, the Cauchy-Schwarz arguments used here are not as efficient in the Type I setting as the Cauchy-Schwarz arguments in the sections below, and so these estimates do not supersede their Type I counterparts.

5.5. Proof of first Type I estimate

We will establish Theorem 5.8(i), which is the easiest of the Type I estimates to prove. The strategy follows closely that of the previous section. The changes, roughly speaking, are that the Cauchy-Schwarz argument is slightly modified (so that only the q2q_{2} variable is duplicated, rather than both q1q_{1} and q2q_{2}) and that we use an exponential sum estimate based on the first part of Corollary 4.16 instead of the second.

by (5.40) and (5.41), that (c2,δ2)/δ2≤1(c_{2},\delta_{2})/\delta_{2}\leq 1 and that (c1,δ)/δ1≤(c1,r)/r(c_{1},\delta)/\delta_{1}\leq(c_{1},r)/r, where inspection of the rr-component of Φ1​(n)​Φ2​(n)¯\Phi_{1}(n)\overline{\Phi_{2}(n)} using (5.29) shows that a prime p|rp\mid r divides c1c_{1} if and only if p|h1​v2−h2​v1p\mid h_{1}v_{2}-h_{2}v_{1}. ∎

6. Trace functions and multidimensional exponential sum estimates

In this section (as in Section 4), we do not use the standard asymptotic convention (Definition 1.2), since we discuss general ideas that are of interest independently of the goal of bounding gaps between primes.

We will discuss some of the machinery and formalism of ℓ\ell-adic sheaves ℱ\mathcal{F} on curves55 5 In our applications, the only curves UU we deal with are obtained by removing a finite number of points from the projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. and their associated Frobenius trace functions tℱt_{\mathcal{F}}. This will allow us to state and then apply the deep theorems of Deligne’s general form of the Riemann Hypothesis over finite fields for such sheaves. We will use these theorems to establish certain estimates for multi-variable exponential sums which go beyond the one-dimensional estimates obtainable from Lemma 4.2 (specifically, the estimates we need are stated in Corollary 6.24 and Corollary 6.26).

The point is that these Frobenius trace functions significantly generalize the rational phase functions x↦ep​(P⁡(x)Q⁡(x))x\mapsto e_{p}\left(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\right) which appear in Lemma 4.2. They include more general functions, such as the hyper-Kloosterman sums

x↦(−1)m−1pm−12​∑⋯∑y1,…,ym∈𝔽py1​…​ym=x⁡ep​(y1+⋯+ym),x\mapsto\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{p^{\frac{m-1}{2}}}\mathop{\sum\cdots\sum}\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\\ y_{1}\ldots y_{m}=x\end{subarray}}e_{p}(y_{1}+\cdots+y_{m}),

and satisfy a very flexible formalism. In particular, the class of Frobenius trace functions is (essentially) closed under basic operations such as pointwise addition and multiplication, complex conjugation, change of variable (pullback), and the normalized Fourier transform. Using these closure properties allows us to build a rich class of useful trace functions from just a small set of basic trace functions. In fact, the sheaves we actually use in this paper are ultimately obtained from only two sheaves: the Artin-Schreier sheaf and the third hyper-Kloosterman sheaf.66 6 One can even reduce the number of generating sheaves to one, because the sheaf-theoretic Fourier transform, combined with pullback via the inversion map x↦1xx\mapsto\frac{1}{x}, may be used to iteratively build the hyper-Kloosterman sheaves from the Artin-Schreier sheaf. However, we have chosen to discuss more general sheaves in this section in order to present the sheaf-theoretic framework in a more natural fashion.

Because exponential sums depending on a parameter are often themselves trace functions, one can recast many multidimensional exponential sums (e.g.

∑x1,…,xn∈𝔽pep​(f⁡(x1,…,xn))\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}e_{p}(f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}))

for some rational function f∈𝔽p​(X1,…,Xn)f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})) in terms of one-dimensional sums of Frobenius trace functions. As a very rough first approximation, Deligne’s results [9] imply that the square root cancellation exhibited in Lemma 4.2 is also present for these more general sums of Frobenius trace functions, as long as certain degenerate cases are avoided. Therefore, at least in principle, this implies square root cancellation for many multidimensional exponential sums.

In practice, this is often not entirely straightforward, as we will explain. One particular issue is that the bounds provided by Deligne’s theorems depend on a certain measure of complexity of the ℓ\ell-adic sheaf defining the trace function, which is known as the conductor of a sheaf. In estimates for sums of trace functions, this conductor plays the same role that the degrees of the polynomials f,gf,g play in Lemma 4.2. We will therefore have to expend some effort to control the conductors of various sheaves before we can extract usable estimates from Deligne’s results.

This section is not self-contained, and assumes a certain amount of prior formal knowledge of the terminology of ℓ\ell-adic cohomology on curves. For readers who are not familiar with this material, we would recommend as references such surveys as [30, §11.11], [35], [20], and some of the books and papers of Katz, in particular [31, 33, 32], as well as Deligne’s own account [7, Sommes trig.]. We would like to stress that, if the main results of the theory are assumed and the construction of some main objects (e.g. the Artin-Schreier and hyper-Kloosterman sheaves) is accepted, working with ℓ\ell-adic sheaves essentially amounts to studying certain finite-dimensional continuous representations of the Galois group of the field 𝔽p​(X)\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) of rational functions over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Alternatively, for the purposes of establishing only the bounds on (incomplete) multi-variable exponential sums used in the proofs of the main theorems of this paper (namely the bounds in Corollary 6.24 and Corollary 6.26), it is possible to ignore all references to sheaves, if one accepts the estimates on complete multi-dimensional exponential sums in Proposition 6.11 and Theorem 6.17 as “black boxes”; the estimates on incomplete exponential sums will be deduced from these results via completion of sums and the qq-van der Corput AA-process.

6.1. ℓ\ell-adic sheaves on the projective line

For pp a prime, we fix an algebraic closure 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and denote by k⊂𝔽p¯=k¯k\subset\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}=\overline{k} a finite extension of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. Its cardinality is usually denoted |k|=p[k:𝔽p]=pdeg⁡(k)=q|k|=p^{[k:\mathbb{F}_{p}]}=p^{\operatorname{deg}(k)}=q. For us, the Frobenius element relative to kk means systematically the geometric Frobenius Frk\mathrm{Fr}_{k}, which is the inverse in Gal(k¯/k)\Gal(\overline{k}/k) of the arithmetic Frobenius, x↦xqx\mapsto x^{q} on k¯\overline{k}.

We denote by K=𝔽p​(t)K=\mathbb{F}_{p}(t) the function field of the projective line ℙ𝔽p1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} and by K¯⊃𝔽p¯\overline{K}\supset\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} some separable closure; let η¯=Spec⁡(K¯)\overline{\eta}=\mathrm{Spec}(\overline{K}) be the corresponding geometric generic point.

We fix another prime ℓ≠p\ell\neq p, and we denote by ι:ℚℓ¯↪ℂ\iota\colon\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C} an algebraic closure of the field ℚℓ\mathbb{Q}_{\ell} of ℓ\ell-adic numbers, together with an embedding into the complex numbers. By an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on a noetherian scheme XX (in practice, a curve), we always mean a constructible sheaf of finite-dimensional ℚℓ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}-vector spaces with respect to the étale topology on XX, and we recall that the category of ℓ\ell-adic sheaves is abelian.

We will be especially interested in the case X=ℙk1X=\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} (the projective line) and we will use the following notation for the translation, dilation, and fractional linear maps from ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} to itself:

[+l]:x\displaystyle[+l]\colon x ↦x+l,\displaystyle\mapsto x+l,
[×a]:x\displaystyle[\times a]\colon x ↦a​x,\displaystyle\mapsto ax,
γ:x\displaystyle\gamma\colon x ↦γ⋅x=a​x+bc​x+d​ for ​γ=(abcd)∈GL2​(𝔽p).\displaystyle\mapsto\gamma\cdot x=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}\text{ for }\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p}).

We will often transform a sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} by applying pullback by one of the above maps, and we denote these pullback sheaves by [+l]∗​ℱ[+l]^{*}\mathcal{F}, [×a]∗ℱ[\times a]^{*}\mathcal{F} and γ∗​ℱ\gamma^{*}\mathcal{F}.

6.1.1. Galois representations

The category of ℓ\ell-adic sheaves on ℙk1\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} admits a relatively concrete description in terms of representations of the Galois group Gal(K¯/k.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/k.K). We recall some important features of it here and we refer to [31, 4.4] for a complete presentation.

For j:U↪ℙk1j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} some non-empty open subset defined over kk, we denote by π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U) (resp. π1g​(U)\pi^{g}_{1}(U)) the arithmetic (resp. geometric) fundamental group of UU, which may be defined as the quotient of Gal(K¯/k.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/k.K) (resp. of Gal(K¯/k¯.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/\overline{k}.K)) by the smallest closed normal subgroup containing all the inertia subgroups above the closed points of UU. We have then a commutative diagram of short exact sequences of groups

(6.1)

Given an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on ℙk1\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1}, there exists some non-empty (hence dense, in the Zariski topology) open set j:U↪ℙk1j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} such that the pullback j∗​ℱj^{*}\mathcal{F} (the restriction of ℱ\mathcal{F} to UU) is lisse, or in other words, for which j∗​ℱj^{*}\mathcal{F} “is” a finite-dimensional continuous representation ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} of Gal(K¯/k.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/k.K) factoring through π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U)

ρℱ:Gal(K¯/k.K)↠π1(U)→GL(ℱη¯),\rho_{\mathcal{F}}\colon\Gal(\overline{K}/k.K)\twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(U)\rightarrow\mathrm{GL}(\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}),

where the geometric generic stalk ℱη¯\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}} of ℱ\mathcal{F} is a finite-dimensional ℚℓ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}-vector space. Its dimension is the (generic) rank of ℱ\mathcal{F} and is denoted rk⁡(ℱ)\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F}). There is a maximal (with respect to inclusion) open subset on which ℱ\mathcal{F} is lisse, which will be denoted UℱU_{\mathcal{F}}.

We will freely apply the terminology of representations to ℓ\ell-adic sheaves. The properties of ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} as a representation of the arithmetic Galois group Gal(K¯/k.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/k.K) (or of the arithmetic fundamental group π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U)) will be qualified as “arithmetic”, while the properties of its restriction ρℱg\rho_{\mathcal{F}}^{g} to the geometric Galois group Gal(K¯/k¯.K)\Gal(\overline{K}/\overline{k}.K) (or the geometric fundamental group π1g​(U)\pi_{1}^{g}(U)) will be qualified as “geometric”. For instance, we will say that ℱ\mathcal{F} is arithmetically irreducible (resp. geometrically irreducible) or arithmetically isotypic (resp. geometrically isotypic) if the corresponding arithmetic representation ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} (resp. the geometric representation ρℱg\rho_{\mathcal{F}}^{g}) is.

We will be mostly interested in the geometric properties of a sheaf, therefore we will usually omit the adjective “geometric” in our statements, so that “isotypic” will mean “geometrically isotypic”. We will always spell out explicitly when an arithmetic property is intended, so that no confusion can arise.

6.1.2. Middle-extension sheaves

An ℓ\ell-adic sheaf is a called a middle-extension sheaf if, for some (and in fact, for any) non-empty open subset j:U↪ℙk1j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} such that j∗​ℱj^{*}\mathcal{F} is lisse, we have an arithmetic isomorphism

ℱ≃j∗​j∗​ℱ,\mathcal{F}\simeq j_{*}j^{*}\mathcal{F},

or equivalently if, for every x¯∈ℙ1​(k¯)\overline{x}\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\overline{k}), the specialization maps (cf. [31, 4.4])

sx¯:ℱx¯→ℱη¯Ix¯s_{\overline{x}}:\mathcal{F}_{\overline{x}}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^{I_{\overline{x}}}

are isomorphisms, where Ix¯I_{\overline{x}} is the inertia subgroup at x¯\overline{x}. Given an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf, its associated middle-extension is the sheaf

ℱme=j∗​j∗​ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{me}}=j_{*}j^{*}\mathcal{F}

for some non-empty open subset j:U↪ℙk1j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} on which ℱ\mathcal{F} is lisse. This sheaf is a middle-extension sheaf, and is (up to arithmetic isomorphism) the unique middle-extension sheaf whose restriction to UU is arithmetically isomorphic to that of ℱ\mathcal{F}. In particular, ℱme\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{me}} does not depend on the choice of UU.

6.2. The trace function of a sheaf

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf on the projective line over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. For each finite extension k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p}, ℱ\mathcal{F} defines a complex valued function

x↦tℱ​(x,k)x\mapsto t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)

on k∪{∞}=ℙ1​(k)k\cup\{\infty\}=\mathbb{P}^{1}(k), which is called the Frobenius trace function, or just trace function, associated with ℱ\mathcal{F} and kk. It is defined by

ℙ1​(k)∋x↦tℱ​(x,k):=ι⁡(Tr⁡(Frx,k|ℱx¯)).\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)\ni x\mapsto t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k):=\iota(\Tr(\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k}|\mathcal{F}_{\overline{x}})).

Here x¯:Spec⁡(k¯)→ℙk1\overline{x}:\mathrm{Spec}(\overline{k})\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} denotes a geometric point above xx, and ℱx¯\mathcal{F}_{\overline{x}} is the stalk of ℱ\mathcal{F} at that point, which is a finite-dimensional ℚℓ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}-vector space on which Gal(k¯/k)\Gal(\overline{k}/k) acts linearly, and Frx,k\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k} denotes the geometric Frobenius of that Galois group. The trace of the action of this operator is independent of the choice of x¯\overline{x}.

If k=𝔽pk=\mathbb{F}_{p}, which is the case of importance for the applications in this paper, we will write tℱ​(x,p)t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;p) or simply tℱ​(x)t_{\mathcal{F}}(x) instead of tℱ​(x,𝔽p)t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;\mathbb{F}_{p}).

If x∈Uℱ​(k)x\in U_{\mathcal{F}}(k), the quantity tℱ​(x,k)t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k) is simply the trace of the geometric Frobenius conjugacy class of a place of K¯\overline{K} above xx acting through the associated representation ℱη¯\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}, i.e., the value (under ι\iota) of the character of the representation at this conjugacy class:

tℱ​(x,k)=ι⁡(Tr⁡(Frx,k|ℱη¯)).t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)=\iota(\Tr(\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k}|\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}})).

If ℱ\mathcal{F} is a middle-extension sheaf one has more generally

tℱ​(x,k)=ι⁡(Tr⁡(Frx,k|ℱη¯Ix¯)).t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)=\iota(\Tr(\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k}|\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^{I_{\overline{x}}})).

For any sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}, the trace function of ℱ\mathcal{F} restricted to Uℱ​(k)U_{\mathcal{F}}(k) coincides with the restriction of the trace function of ℱme\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{me}}.

6.2.1. Purity and admissibility

The following notion was introduced by Deligne [9].

Definition 6.1 (Purity).

For i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf on ℙ𝔽p1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} is generically pure (or pure, for short) of weight ii if, for any k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and any x∈Uℱ​(k)x\in U_{\mathcal{F}}(k), the eigenvalues of Frx,k\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k} acting on ℱη¯\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}} are ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebraic numbers whose Galois conjugates have complex absolute value equal to qi/2=|k|i/2q^{i/2}=|k|^{i/2}.

Remark 6.2.

Deligne proved (see [9, (1.8.9)]) that if ℱ\mathcal{F} is generically pure of weight ii, then for any k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and any x∈ℙ1​(k)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(k), the eigenvalues of Frx,k\mathrm{Fr}_{x,k} acting on ℱη¯Ix¯\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^{I_{\overline{x}}} are ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebraic numbers whose Galois conjugates have complex absolute value ≤qi/2\leq q^{i/2}.

In particular, if ℱ\mathcal{F} is a middle-extension sheaf which is pointwise pure of weight ii, then we get

|tℱ​(x,k)|=|ι⁡(Tr⁡(Frx|ℱη¯Ix¯))|≤rk⁡(ℱ)​qi/2|t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)|=|\iota(\Tr(\mathrm{Fr}_{x}|\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^{I_{\overline{x}}}))|\leq\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F})q^{i/2} (6.2)

for any x∈ℙ1​(k)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(k).

We can now describe the class of sheaves and trace functions that we will work with.

Definition 6.3 (Admissible sheaves).

Let kk be a finite extension of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. An admissible sheaf over kk is a middle-extension sheaf on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} which is pointwise pure of weight 00. An admissible trace function over kk is a function k→ℂk\rightarrow\mathbb{C} which is equal to the trace function of some admissible sheaf restricted to k⊂ℙ1​(k)k\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}(k).

Remark 6.4.

The weight 00 condition may be viewed as a normalization to ensure that admissible trace functions typically have magnitude comparable to 11. Sheaves which are pure of some other weight can be studied by reducing to the 00 case by the simple device of Tate twists. However, we will not need to do this, as we will be working exclusively with sheaves which are pure of weight 00.

6.2.2. Conductor

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a middle-extension sheaf on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}. The conductor of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined to be

cond(ℱ):=rk⁡(ℱ)+|(ℙ1−Uℱ)​(k¯)|+∑x∈(ℙ1−Uℱ)​(k¯)swanx⁡(ℱ)\cond(\mathcal{F}):=\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F})+|(\mathbb{P}^{1}-U_{\mathcal{F}})(\overline{k})|+\sum_{x\in(\mathbb{P}^{1}-U_{\mathcal{F}})(\overline{k})}\swan_{x}(\mathcal{F})

where swanx⁡(ℱ)\swan_{x}(\mathcal{F}) denotes the Swan conductor of the representation ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} at xx, a non-negative integer measuring the “wild ramification” of ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} at xx (see e.g. [32, Definition 1.6] for the precise definition of the Swan conductor). If swanx⁡(ℱ)=0\swan_{x}(\mathcal{F})=0, one says that ℱ\mathcal{F} is tamely ramified at xx, and otherwise that it is wildly ramified.

The invariant cond(ℱ)\cond(\mathcal{F}) is a non-negative integer (positive if ℱ≠0\mathcal{F}\neq 0) and it measures the complexity of the sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} and of its trace function tℱt_{\mathcal{F}}. For instance, if ℱ\mathcal{F} is admissible, so that it is also pure of weight 00, then we deduce from (6.2) that

|tℱ​(x,k)|≤rk⁡(ℱ)≤cond(ℱ)|t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)|\leq\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F})\leq\cond(\mathcal{F}) (6.3)

for any x∈kx\in k.

6.2.3. Dual and Tensor Product

Given admissible sheaves ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}, their tensor product, denoted ℱ⊗𝒢\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G}, is by definition the middle-extension sheaf associated to the tensor product representation ρℱ⊗ρ𝒢\rho_{\mathcal{F}}\otimes\rho_{\mathcal{G}} (computed over the intersection of UℱU_{\mathcal{F}} and U𝒢U_{\mathcal{G}}, which is still a dense open set of ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}). Note that this sheaf may be different from the tensor product of ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} as constructible sheaves (similarly to the fact that the product of two primitive Dirichlet characters is not necessarily primitive).

Similarly, the dual of ℱ\mathcal{F}, denoted ℱˇ\widecheck{\mathcal{F}}, is defined as the middle extension sheaf associated to the contragredient representation ρℱˇ\widecheck{\rho_{\mathcal{F}}}.

We have

Uℱ∩U𝒢⊂Uℱ⊗𝒢,Uℱˇ=Uℱ.U_{\mathcal{F}}\cap U_{\mathcal{G}}\subset U_{\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G}},\quad\quad U_{\widecheck{\mathcal{F}}}=U_{\mathcal{F}}.

It is not obvious, but true, that the tensor product and the dual of admissible sheaves are admissible. We then have

tℱ⊗𝒢​(x,k)=tℱ​(x,k)​t𝒢​(x,k),tℱˇ​(x,k)=tℱ​(x,k)¯t_{\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G}}(x;k)=t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)t_{\mathcal{G}}(x;k),\quad\quad t_{\widecheck{\mathcal{F}}}(x;k)=\overline{t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)} (6.4)

for x∈Uℱ​(k)∩U𝒢​(k)x\in U_{\mathcal{F}}(k)\cap U_{\mathcal{G}}(k) and x∈ℙ1​(k)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(k), respectively. In particular, the product of two admissible trace functions tℱt_{\mathcal{F}} and t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} coincides with an admissible trace function outside a set of at most cond(ℱ)+cond(𝒢)\cond(\mathcal{F})+\cond(\mathcal{G}) elements, and the complex conjugate of an admissible trace function is again an admissible trace function.

We also have

cond(ℱˇ)=cond(ℱ)\cond(\widecheck{\mathcal{F}})=\cond(\mathcal{F}) (6.5)

(which is easy to check from the definition of Swan conductors) and

cond(ℱ⊗𝒢)≪rk(ℱ)rk(𝒢)cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢)≤cond(ℱ)2cond(𝒢)2\cond(\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G})\ll\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F})\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{G})\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G})\leq\cond(\mathcal{F})^{2}\cond(\mathcal{G})^{2} (6.6)

where the implied constant is absolute (which is also relatively elementary, see [15, Prop. 8.2(2)] or [19, Lemma 4.8]).

6.3. Irreducible components and isotypic decomposition

Let kk be a finite field, let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an admissible sheaf over ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} and consider U=UℱU=U_{\mathcal{F}} and the corresponding open immersion j:U↪ℙk1j\colon U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}. A fundamental result of Deligne [9, (3.4.1)] proves that ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} is then geometrically semisimple. Thus there exist lisse sheaves 𝒢\mathcal{G} on U×k¯U\times\overline{k}, irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic, and integers n⁡(𝒢)≥1n(\mathcal{G})\geq 1, such that we have

j∗​ℱ≃⨁𝒢𝒢n⁡(𝒢)j^{*}\mathcal{F}\simeq\bigoplus_{\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{G}^{n(\mathcal{G})}

as an isomorphism of lisse sheaves on U×k¯U\times\overline{k} (the 𝒢\mathcal{G} might not be defined over kk). Extending with j∗j_{*} to ℙk¯1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\overline{k}} we obtain a decomposition

ℱ≃⨁𝒢j∗​𝒢n⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{F}\simeq\bigoplus_{\mathcal{G}}j_{*}\mathcal{G}^{n(\mathcal{G})}

where each j∗​𝒢j_{*}\mathcal{G} is a middle-extension sheaf over k¯\overline{k}. We call the sheaves j∗​𝒢j_{*}\mathcal{G} the geometrically irreducible components of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Over the open set UℱU_{\mathcal{F}}, we can define the arithmetic semisimplification ρℱss\rho_{\mathcal{F}}^{\text{ss}} as the direct sum of the Jordan-Hölder arithmetically irreducible components of the representation ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}}. Each arithmetically irreducible component is either geometrically isotypic or induced from a proper finite index subgroup of π1​(Uℱ)\pi_{1}(U_{\mathcal{F}}). If an arithmetically irreducible component π\pi is induced, it follows that the trace function of the middle-extension sheaf corresponding to π\pi vanishes identically. Thus, if we denote by Iso⁡(ℱ)\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{F}) the set of middle-extensions associated to the geometrically isotypic components of ρℱss\rho_{\mathcal{F}}^{\text{ss}}, we obtain an identity

tℱ=∑𝒢∈Iso⁡(ℱ)t𝒢t_{\mathcal{F}}=\sum_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{F})}t_{\mathcal{G}} (6.7)

(indeed, these two functions coincide on UℱU_{\mathcal{F}} and are both trace functions of middle-extension sheaves), where each summand is admissible. For these facts, we refer to [31, §4.4, §4.5] and [15, Prop. 8.3].

6.4. Deligne’s main theorem and quasi-orthogonality

The generalizations of complete exponential sums over finite fields that we consider are sums

S⁡(ℱ,k)=∑x∈ktℱ​(x,k)S(\mathcal{F};k)=\sum_{x\in k}t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)

for any admissible sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}. By (6.3), we have the trivial bound

|S(ℱ;k)|≤cond(ℱ)|k|=cond(ℱ)q.|S(\mathcal{F};k)|\leq\cond(\mathcal{F})|k|=\cond(\mathcal{F})q.

Deligne’s main theorem [9, Thm. 1] provides strong non-trivial estimates for such sums, at least when pp is large compared to cond(ℱ)\cond(\mathcal{F}).

Theorem 6.5 (Sums of trace functions).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an admissible sheaf on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} where |k|=q|k|=q and U=UℱU=U_{\mathcal{F}}. We have

S(ℱ;k)=qTr(Frk|(ℱη¯)π1g​(U))+O(cond(ℱ)2q1/2)S(\mathcal{F};k)=q\Tr\left(\mathrm{Fr}_{k}|(\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}})_{\pi_{1}^{g}(U)}\right)+O(\cond(\mathcal{F})^{2}q^{1/2})

where (ℱη¯)π1g​(U)(\mathcal{F}_{\overline{\eta}})_{\pi_{1}^{g}(U)} denotes the Tate-twisted π1g​(Uℱ)\pi_{1}^{g}(U_{\mathcal{F}})-coinvariant space77 7 Recall that the coinvariant space of a representation of a group GG is the largest quotient on which the group GG acts trivially. of ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}}, on which Gal(k¯/k)\Gal(\overline{k}/k) acts canonically, and where the implied constant is effective and absolute.

Using (6.3), we have

6.4.1. Correlation and quasi-orthogonality of trace functions

An important application of the above formula arises when estimating the correlation between the trace functions tℱt_{\mathcal{F}} and t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} associated to two admissible sheaves ℱ,𝒢\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}, i.e., when computing the sum associated to the tensor product sheaf ℱ⊗𝒢ˇ\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}}. We define the correlation sum

C⁡(ℱ,𝒢,k):=∑x∈ktℱ​(x,k)​t𝒢​(x,k)¯.C(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G};k):=\sum_{x\in k}t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)\overline{t_{\mathcal{G}}(x;k)}.

From (6.3) we have the trivial bound

|Cℱ,𝒢(k)|≤cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢)q.|C_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}}(k)|\leq\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G})q.

The Riemann Hypothesis allows us improve upon this bound when ℱ\mathcal{F}, 𝒢\mathcal{G} are “disjoint”:

Corollary 6.6 (Square root cancellation).

Let ℱ,𝒢\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G} be two admissible sheaves on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} for a finite field kk. If ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} have no irreducible constituent in common, then we have

|C(ℱ,𝒢;k)|≪(cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢))4q1/2|C(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G};k)|\ll(\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G}))^{4}q^{1/2}

where the implied constant is absolute. In particular, if in addition cond(ℱ)\cond(\mathcal{F}) and cond(𝒢)\cond(\mathcal{G}) are bounded by a fixed constant, then

|C⁡(ℱ,𝒢,k)|≪q1/2.|C(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G};k)|\ll q^{1/2}.
Proof.

We have

tℱ⊗𝒢ˇ​(x,k)=tℱ​(x,k)​t𝒢​(x,k)¯t_{\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}}}(x;k)=t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)\overline{t_{\mathcal{G}}(x;k)}

for x∈Uℱ​(k)∩U𝒢​(k)x\in U_{\mathcal{F}}(k)\cap U_{\mathcal{G}}(k) and

|tℱ⊗𝒢ˇ(x;k)|,|tℱ(x;k)t𝒢​(x,k)¯|≤cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢).|t_{\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}}}(x;k)|,\quad|t_{\mathcal{F}}(x;k)\overline{t_{\mathcal{G}}(x;k)}|\leq\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G}).

Thus the previous proposition applied to the sheaf ℱ⊗𝒢ˇ\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}} gives

C⁡(ℱ,𝒢,k)\displaystyle C(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G};k) =S(ℱ⊗𝒢ˇ;k)+O((cond(ℱ)+cond(𝒢))cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢))\displaystyle=S(\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}};k)+O((\cond(\mathcal{F})+\cond(\mathcal{G}))\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G}))
=qTr(Frk|(ℱ⊗𝒢ˇ)η¯)π1g​(U))+O((cond(ℱ)cond(𝒢))4q1/2)\displaystyle=q\Tr\left(\mathrm{Fr}_{k}|(\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{G}})_{\overline{\eta}})_{\pi_{1}^{g}(U)}\right)+O((\cond(\mathcal{F})\cond(\mathcal{G}))^{4}q^{1/2})

using (6.5) and (6.6). We conclude by observing that, by Schur’s Lemma and the geometric semisimplicity of admissible sheaves (proved by Deligne [9, (3.4.1)]), our disjointness assumption on ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} implies that the coinvariant space vanishes. ∎

6.5. The Artin-Schreier sheaf

We will now start discussing specific important admissible sheaves. Let pp be a prime and let ψ:(𝔽p,+)→ℂ×\psi\colon(\mathbb{F}_{p},+)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times} be a non-trivial additive character. For any finite extension kk of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, we then have an additive character

ψk:{k→ℂ×x↦ψ⁡(Trk/𝔽p⁡(x)),\psi_{k}\colon\begin{cases}k\to\mathbb{C}^{\times}\\ x\mapsto\psi(\Tr_{k/\mathbb{F}_{p}}(x)),\end{cases}

where Trk/𝔽p\Tr_{k/\mathbb{F}_{p}} is the trace map from kk to 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

One shows (see [32, Chap. 4], [7, §1.4], [30, p. 302–303]) that there exists an admissible sheaf ℒψ\mathcal{L}_{\psi}, called the Artin-Schreier sheaf associated to ψ\psi, with the following properties:

  • •

    the sheaf ℒψ\mathcal{L}_{\psi} has rank 11, hence is automatically geometrically irreducible, and it is geometrically non-trivial;

  • •

    the sheaf ℒψ\mathcal{L}_{\psi} is lisse on 𝔸𝔽p1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}, and wildly ramified at ∞\infty with swan∞⁡(ℒψ)=1\swan_{\infty}(\mathcal{L}_{\psi})=1, so that in particular cond(ℒψ)=3\cond(\mathcal{L}_{\psi})=3, independently of pp and of the non-trivial additive character ψ\psi;

  • •

    the trace function is given by the formula

    tℒψ​(x,k)=ψk​(x)t_{\mathcal{L}_{\psi}}(x;k)=\psi_{k}(x)

    for every finite extension k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and every x∈𝔸1​(k)=kx\in\mathbb{A}^{1}(k)=k, and

    tℒψ​(∞,k)=0.t_{\mathcal{L}_{\psi}}(\infty;k)=0.

Let f∈𝔽p​(X)f\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X) be a rational function not of the shape gp−g+cg^{p}-g+c for g∈𝔽p​(X),c∈𝔽pg\in\mathbb{F}_{p}(X),\ c\in\mathbb{F}_{p} (for instance whose zeros or poles have order prime to pp). Then ff defines a morphism f:ℙ𝔽p1→ℙ𝔽p1f\colon\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}, and we denote by ℒψ⁡(f)\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)} the pull-back sheaf f∗​ℒψf^{*}\mathcal{L}_{\psi}, which we call the Artin-Schreier sheaf associated to ff and ψ\psi. Then ℒψ⁡(f)\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)} has the following properties:

  • •

    it has rank 11, hence is geometrically irreducible, and it is geometrically non-trivial (because ff is not of the form gp−g+cg^{p}-g+c for some other function gg, by assumption);

  • •

    it is lisse outside the poles of ff, and wildly ramified at each pole with Swan conductor equal to the order of the pole, so that if the denominator of ff has degree dd (coprime to pp) we have cond(ℒψ⁡(f))=1+e+d\cond(\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)})=1+e+d, where ee is the number of distinct poles of ff;

  • •

    it has trace function given by the formula

    tℒψ⁡(f)​(x,k)=ψ⁡(trk/𝔽p​(f⁡(x)))t_{\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)}}(x;k)=\psi(\mathrm{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_{p}}(f(x)))

    for any finite extension k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and any x∈ℙ1​(k)x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(k) which is not a pole of ff, and tℒψ⁡(f)​(x,k)=0t_{\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)}}(x;k)=0 if xx is a pole of ff.

In particular, from Theorem 6.5, we thus obtain the estimate

|∑x∈𝔽pψ⁡(f⁡(x))|≪deg⁡(f)2​p1/2\Bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\psi(f(x))\Bigr|\ll\deg(f)^{2}p^{1/2}

for such ff, which is a slightly weaker form of the Weil bound from Lemma 4.2. Note that this weakening, which is immaterial in our applications, is only due to the general formulation of Theorem 6.5 which did not attempt to obtain the best possible estimate for specific situations.

6.6. The ℓ\ell-adic Fourier transform

Let pp be a prime, k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} a finite extension and ψ\psi a non-trivial additive character of kk. For a finite extension k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and a function x↦t⁡(x)x\mapsto t(x) defined on kk, we define the normalized Fourier transform FTψ​t​(x)\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}t(x) by the formula

FTψt(x):=−1q1/2∑y∈kt(y)ψ(xy)\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}t(x):=-\frac{1}{q^{1/2}}\sum_{y\in k}t(y)\psi(xy)

(which is similar to (4.11) except for the sign). It is a very deep fact that, when applied to trace functions, this construction has a sheaf-theoretic incarnation. This was defined by Deligne and studied extensively by Laumon [36] and Katz [32]. However, a restriction on the admissible sheaves is necessary, in view of the following obstruction: if t⁡(x)=ψ⁡(b​x)t(x)=\psi(bx) for some b∈kb\in k, then its Fourier transform is a Dirac-type function

FTψ​(t)​(x)=−q1/2​δ−b​(x)={−q1/2 if x=−b0 otherwise.\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(t)(x)=-q^{1/2}\delta_{-b}(x)=\begin{cases}-q^{1/2}&\text{ if $x=-b$}\\ 0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

But this cannot in general be an admissible trace function with bounded conductor as this would violate (6.2) at x=−bx=-b if qq is large enough. We make the following definition, as in [32]:

Definition 6.7 (Admissible Fourier sheaves).

An admissible sheaf over ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} is a Fourier sheaf if its geometrically irreducible components are neither trivial nor Artin-Schreier sheaves ℒψ\mathcal{L}_{\psi} for some non-trivial additive character ψ\psi.

Theorem 6.8 (Sheaf-theoretic Fourier transform).

Let pp be a prime and k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} a finite extension, and let ψ\psi be a non-trivial additive character of kk. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an admissible ℓ\ell-adic Fourier sheaf on ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k}. There exists an ℓ\ell-adic sheaf

𝒢=FTψ​(ℱ),\mathcal{G}=\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(\mathcal{F}),

called the Fourier transform of ℱ\mathcal{F}, which is also an admissible ℓ\ell-adic Fourier sheaf, with the property that for any finite extension k′/kk^{\prime}/k, we have

t𝒢​(⋅,k′)=FTψk′​tℱ​(⋅,k),t_{\mathcal{G}}(\cdot;k^{\prime})=\mathrm{FT}_{\psi_{k^{\prime}}}t_{\mathcal{F}}(\cdot;k),

in particular

t𝒢(x;k)=−1|k|∑y∈ktℱ(y;k)ψ(xy).t_{\mathcal{G}}(x;k)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{|k|}}\sum_{y\in k}t_{\mathcal{F}}(y;k)\psi(xy).

Moreover, the following additional assertions hold:

  • •

    The sheaf 𝒢\mathcal{G} is geometrically irreducible, or geometrically isotypic, if and only if ℱ\mathcal{F} is;

  • •

    The Fourier transform is (almost) involutive, in the sense that we have a canonical arithmetic isomorphism

    FTψ𝒢≃[×(−1)]∗ℱ\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}\mathcal{G}\simeq[\times(-1)]^{*}\mathcal{F} (6.8)

    where [×(−1)]∗[\times(-1)]^{*} denotes the pull-back by the map x↦−xx\mapsto-x;

  • •

    We have

    cond(𝒢)≤10cond(ℱ)2.\cond(\mathcal{G})\leq 10\cond(\mathcal{F})^{2}. (6.9)
Proof.

These claims are established for instance in [32, Chap. 8], with the exception of (6.9) which is proved in [15, Prop. 8.2(1)]. ∎

6.7. Kloosterman sheaves

Given a prime p≥3p\geq 3, a non-trivial additive character ψ\psi of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and an integer m≥1m\geq 1, the mthm^{\operatorname{th}} hyper-Kloosterman sums are defined by the formula

Klm⁡(x;k):=1qm−12​∑y1⋯ym=xy1,⋯,ym∈kψk​(y1+⋯+ym)\hypk_{m}(x;k):=\frac{1}{q^{\frac{m-1}{2}}}\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\scriptstyle y_{1},\cdots,y_{m}\in k}}}{{{\scriptstyle y_{1}\cdots y_{m}=x}}}}\psi_{k}(y_{1}+\cdots+y_{m}) (6.10)

for any finite extension k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and any x∈kx\in k. Thus, we have for instance Kl1⁡(x;k)=ψk​(x)\hypk_{1}(x;k)=\psi_{k}(x), while Kl2\hypk_{2} is essentially a classical Kloosterman sum.

The following deep result shows that, as functions of xx, these sums are trace functions of admissible sheaves.

Proposition 6.9 (Deligne; Katz).

There exists an admissible Fourier sheaf 𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m} such that, for any k/𝔽pk/\mathbb{F}_{p} and any x∈k×x\in k^{\times}, we have

t𝒦​ℓm​(x,k)=(−1)m−1​Klm⁡(x;k).t_{\mathcal{K}\ell_{m}}(x;k)=(-1)^{m-1}\hypk_{m}(x;k).

Furthermore:

  • •

    𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m} is lisse on 𝔾m=ℙ1−{0,∞}\mathbb{G}_{m}=\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0,\infty\}; if m≥2m\geq 2, it is tamely ramified at 00, and for m=1m=1 it is lisse at 00; for all m≥1m\geq 1, it is wildly ramified at ∞\infty with Swan conductor 11;

  • •

    𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m} is of rank mm, and is geometrically irreducible;

  • •

    if pp is odd, then the Zariski closure of the image ρ𝒦​ℓm​(π1g​(𝔾m))\rho_{\mathcal{K}\ell_{m}}(\pi^{g}_{1}(\mathbb{G}_{m})), which is called the geometric monodromy group of 𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m}, is isomorphic to SLm\mathrm{SL}_{m} if mm is odd, and to Spm\mathrm{Sp}_{m} if mm is even.

It follows that cond(𝒦​ℓm)=m+3\cond(\mathcal{K}\ell_{m})=m+3 for all m≥2m\geq 2 and all pp, and that cond(𝒦​ℓ1)=3\cond(\mathcal{K}\ell_{1})=3.

Proof.

All these results can be found in the book of Katz [32]; more precisely, the first two points are part of Theorem 4.1.1 in [32] and the last is part of Theorem 11.1 in the same reference. ∎

Remark 6.10.

In particular, for x≠0x\neq 0, we get the estimate

|Klm⁡(x;k)|≤m,|\hypk_{m}(x;k)|\leq m,

first proved by Deligne. Note that this exhibits square-root cancellation in the (m−1)(m-1)-variable character sum defining Kl⁡(x,k)\hypk(x;k). For x=0x=0, it is elementary that

Klm(0;k)=(−1)m−1q−(m−1)/2.\hypk_{m}(0;k)=(-1)^{m-1}q^{-(m-1)/2}.

We have the following bounds for hyper-Kloosterman sums, where the case m=3m=3 is the important one for this paper:

Proposition 6.11 (Estimates for hyper-Kloosterman sums).

Let m≥2m\geq 2 be an integer, and ψ′\psi^{\prime} an additive character of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, which may be trivial. We have

|∑x∈𝔽p×Klm⁡(x;p)​ψ′​(x)|≪p1/2.\Bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}\hypk_{m}(x;p)\psi^{\prime}(x)\Bigr|\ll p^{1/2}. (6.11)

Further, let a∈𝔽p×a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}. If either a≠1a\neq 1 or ψ′\psi^{\prime} is non-trivial, we have

|∑x∈𝔽p×Klm⁡(x;p)​Klm⁡(a​x,p)¯​ψ′​(x)|≪p1/2\Bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}}\hypk_{m}(x;p)\overline{\hypk_{m}(ax;p)}\psi^{\prime}(x)\Bigr|\ll p^{1/2} (6.12)

In these bounds, the implied constants depend only, and at most polynomially, on mm.

The first bound (6.11) follows directly from Corollary 6.6 and (6.6) because 𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m} is, for m≥2m\geq 2, geometrically irreducible of rank >1>1, and therefore not geometrically isomorphic to the rank 11 Artin-Schreier sheaf ℒψ′\mathcal{L}_{\psi^{\prime}}.

For the proof of (6.12), we use the identity88 8 One could use this identity to recursively build the hyper-Kloosterman sheaf from the Artin-Schreier sheaf, Theorem 6.8, and pullback via the map x↦1xx\mapsto\frac{1}{x}, if desired.

=∑y≠0,−1/by∈𝔽p,Klm−1⁡(y;p)​Klm−1⁡(γ⋅y,p)¯\displaystyle=\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\scriptstyle y\in\mathbb{F}_{p},}}}{{{\scriptstyle y\neq 0,-1/b}}}}\hypk_{m-1}(y;p)\overline{\hypk_{m-1}(\gamma\cdot y;p)}

Remark 6.12.

A similar result was proved by Michel using a different method in [39, Cor. 2.9]. That method requires more information (the knowledge of the geometric monodromy group of 𝒦​ℓm\mathcal{K}\ell_{m}) but gives more general estimates. The case m=3m=3 is (somewhat implicitly) the result used by Friedlander and Iwaniec in [21], which is proved by Birch and Bombieri in the Appendix to [21] (with in fact two proofs, which are rather different and somewhat more ad-hoc than the argument presented here). This same estimate is used by Zhang [52] to control Type III sums.

6.8. The van der Corput method for trace functions

Let t=tℱt=t_{\mathcal{F}} be the trace function associated to an admissible sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}. In the spirit of Proposition 4.12, the qq-van der Corput method, when applied to incomplete sums of tt, followed by completion of sums, produces expressions of the form

∑x∈𝔽pt⁡(x)​t⁡(x+l)¯​ψ​(h​x)\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}t(x)\overline{t(x+l)}\psi(hx)

for (h,l)∈𝔽p×𝔽p×(h,l)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}, and for some additive character ψ\psi. We seek sufficient conditions that ensure square-root cancellation in the above sum, for any l≠0l\neq 0 and any hh.

Observe that if

t⁡(x)=ψ⁡(a​x2+b​x),t(x)=\psi(ax^{2}+bx),

then the sum is sometimes of size pp. Precisely, this happens if and only if h=2​a​lh=2al. As we shall see, this phenomenon is essentially the only obstruction to square-root cancellation.

Definition 6.13 (No polynomial phase).

For a finite field kk and d≥0d\geq 0, we say that an admissible sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over ℙk1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{k} has no polynomial phase of degree ≤d\leq d if no geometrically irreducible component of ℱ\mathcal{F} is geometrically isomorphic to a sheaf of the form ℒψ⁡(P⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{\psi(P(x))} where P​(X)∈𝔽p​[X]P(X)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X] is a polynomial of degree ≤d\leq d.

Thus, for instance, an admissible sheaf is Fourier if and only if it has no polynomial phase of degree ≤1\leq 1.

Remark 6.14.

An obvious sufficient condition for ℱ\mathcal{F} not to contain any polynomial phase (of any degree) is that each geometrically irreducible component of ℱ\mathcal{F} be irreducible of rank ≥2\geq 2, for instance that ℱ\mathcal{F} itself be geometrically irreducible of rank ≥2\geq 2.

The following inverse theorem is a variant of an argument of Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel [17, Lemma 5.4].

Theorem 6.15.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be an integer, and let pp be a prime such that p>dp>d. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an isotypic admissible sheaf over ℙ𝔽p1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} with no polynomial phase of degree ≤d\leq d. Then either cond(ℱ)≥p+1\cond(\mathcal{F})\geq p+1, or for any l∈𝔽p×l\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times} the sheaf ℱ⊗[+l]∗​ℱˇ\mathcal{F}\otimes[+l]^{*}\widecheck{\mathcal{F}} contains no polynomial phase of degree ≤d−1\leq d-1.

In all cases, for any l∈𝔽p×l\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times} and any P​(X)∈𝔽p​[X]P(X)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[X] of degree d−1d-1, we have

|∑x∈𝔽ptℱ​(x+l)​tℱ​(x)¯​ψ​(P⁡(x))|≪p1/2\Bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}t_{\mathcal{F}}(x+l)\overline{t_{\mathcal{F}}(x)}\psi(P(x))\Bigr|\ll p^{1/2} (6.13)

where the implied constant depends, at most polynomially, on cond(ℱ)\cond(\mathcal{F}) and on dd. Furthermore, this estimate holds also if l=0l=0 and P⁡(x)=h​xP(x)=hx with h≠0h\neq 0.

Proof.

First suppose that l≠0l\neq 0. Observe that if cond(ℱ)≥p+1\cond(\mathcal{F})\geq p+1, the bound (6.13) follows from the trivial bound

|tℱ​(x+l)​tℱ​(x)¯​ψ​(P⁡(x))|≤rk​(ℱ)2≤cond(ℱ)2,|t_{\mathcal{F}}(x+l)\overline{t_{\mathcal{F}}(x)}\psi(P(x))|\leq\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F})^{2}\leq\cond(\mathcal{F})^{2},

and that if the sheaf [+l]∗​ℱ⊗ℱˇ[+l]^{*}\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{F}} contains no polynomial phase of degree ≤d−1\leq d-1, then the bound is a consequence of Corollary 6.6.

We now prove that one of these two properties holds. We assume that [+l]∗​ℱ⊗ℱˇ[+l]^{*}\mathcal{F}\otimes\widecheck{\mathcal{F}} contains a polynomial phase of degree ≤d−1\leq d-1, and will deduce that cond(ℱ)≥p+1\cond(\mathcal{F})\geq p+1.

If 𝒢\mathcal{G} is ramified at some point x∈𝔸1​(k¯)x\in\mathbb{A}^{1}(\overline{k}), then since ℒψ⁡(P⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{\psi(P(x))} is lisse on 𝔸1​(k¯)\mathbb{A}^{1}(\overline{k}), we conclude by iterating (6.14) that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is ramified at x,x+l,x+2​l,⋯,x+(p−1)​lx,x+l,\ x+2l,\cdots,x+(p-1)l, which implies that cond(ℱ)≥cond(𝒢)≥p+rk⁡(𝒢)\cond(\mathcal{F})\geq\cond(\mathcal{G})\geq p+\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{G}). Remark 6.16.

For later use, we observe that the property of having no polynomial phase of degree ≤2\leq 2 of an admissible sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} is invariant under the following transformations:

  • •

    Twists by an Artin-Schreier sheaf associated to a polynomial phase of degree ≤2\leq 2, i.e., ℱ↦ℱ⊗ℒψ⁡(a​x2+b​x)\mathcal{F}\mapsto\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{\psi(ax^{2}+bx)};

  • •

    Dilations and translations: ℱ↦[×a]∗ℱ\mathcal{F}\mapsto[\times a]^{*}\mathcal{F} and ℱ↦[+b]∗​ℱ\mathcal{F}\mapsto[+b]^{*}\mathcal{F} where a∈𝔽p×a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times} and b∈𝔽pb\in\mathbb{F}_{p};

  • •

    Fourier transforms, if ℱ\mathcal{F} is Fourier: ℱ↦FTψ​ℱ\mathcal{F}\mapsto\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}\mathcal{F}. Indeed, the Fourier transform of a sheaf ℒψ⁡(P⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{\psi(P(x))} with deg⁡(P)=2\deg(P)=2 is geometrically isomorphic to ℒψ⁡(Q⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{\psi(Q(x))} for some polynomial QQ of degree 22.

Remark 6.18.

Another natural strategy for proving this theorem would be to start with the observation that the function x↦Kf​(x,k)x\mapsto K_{f}(x;k) is the trace function of the constructible ℓ\ell-adic sheaf

𝒦f=R1π1,!ℒψ⁡(f)(1/2),ℒψ⁡(f)=f∗ℒψ\mathcal{K}_{f}=R^{1}\pi_{1,!}\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)}(1/2),\quad\quad\mathcal{L}_{\psi(f)}=f^{*}\mathcal{L}_{\psi}

where π1:𝔸𝔽p2→𝔸𝔽p1\pi_{1}:\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} is the projection on the first coordinate and R1π1,!R^{1}\pi_{1,!} denotes the operation of higher-direct image with compact support associated to that map (and (1/2)(1/2) is a Tate twist). This is known to be mixed of weights ≤0\leq 0 by Deligne’s work [9], and it follows from the general results99 9 Which were partly motivated by the current paper. of Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel in [19] that the conductor of this sheaf is absolutely bounded as pp varies. To fully implement this approach, it would still remain to prove that the weight 00 part of 𝒦f\mathcal{K}_{f} is geometrically irreducible with no polynomial phase of degree ≤2\leq 2. Although such arguments might be necessary in more advanced cases, the direct approach we have taken is simpler here.

Remark 6.19.

In the remainder of this paper, we will only use the bounds (6.17) and (6.18) from Theorem 6.17. These bounds can also be expressed in terms of the Fourier transform FTψ​(Kf)\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(K_{f}) of KfK_{f}, since they are equivalent to

|FTψ​(Kf)​(h)|≪p1/2|\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(K_{f})(h)|\ll p^{1/2}

and

|∑x∈𝔽pFTψ​(Kf)​(x+h)​FTψ​(Kf)​(x)¯​ψ​(−l​x)|≪p1/2,\Bigl|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(K_{f})(x+h)\overline{\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(K_{f})(x)}\psi(-lx)\Bigr|\ll p^{1/2},

respectively. As such, we see that it is in fact enough to show that FTψ​(Kf)\mathrm{FT}_{\psi}(K_{f}), rather than KfK_{f}, is the trace function of a geometrically irreducible admissible sheaf with bounded conductor and no quadratic phase component. Thus, in principle, we could avoid any use of Theorem 6.8 in our arguments (provided that we took the existence of the Kloosterman sheaves for granted). However, from a conceptual point of view, the fact that KfK_{f} has a good trace function interpretation is more important than the corresponding fact for FTψ\mathrm{FT}_{\psi} (for instance, the iterated van der Corput bounds in Remark 6.23 rely on the former fact rather than the latter).

6.10.1. A generalization of Proposition 4.12

Thanks to the square root cancellation for complete sums of trace functions provided by Corollary 6.6, we may extend Proposition 4.12 to general admissible trace functions to squarefree moduli.

    (one van der Corput + Deligne) Assume that, for every p|qp|q, the sheaf ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} has no polynomial phase of degree ≤2\leq 2. Then, for any factorization q=r​sq=rs and N≤qN\leq q, we have

    |∑nψN​(n)​t​(n,q)|≪qε​(N1/2​r1/2+N1/2​s1/4).\Bigl|\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)t(n;q)\Bigr|\ll q^{\varepsilon}\Bigl(N^{1/2}r^{1/2}+N^{1/2}s^{1/4}\Bigr). (6.22)

In all cases the implied constants depend on ε\varepsilon, cond(𝓕)\cond(\text{\boldmath${\mathcal{F}}$}) and the implied constants in the estimates for the derivatives of ψ\psi.

Remark 6.21.

In the context of Proposition 4.12, where t⁡(n,q)=eq​(P⁡(n)Q⁡(n))t(n;q)=e_{q}\left(\frac{P(n)}{Q(n)}\right), the assumptions deg⁡P<deg⁡Q\deg P<\deg Q and deg⁡(Q⁡(p))=deg⁡(Q)\deg(Q\ (p))=\deg(Q) (for all p|qp\mid q), ensure that the sheaves ℒep​(qp¯​P⁡(x)Q⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{e_{p}\left(\overline{q_{p}}\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\right)} do not contain any polynomial phase of any degree.

Remark 6.22.

For future reference, we observe that, in the proof of (6.22) below, we will not use any of the properties of the functions x↦t⁡(x,p)x\mapsto t(x;p) for p|rp\mid r for a given factorization q=r​sq=rs, except for their boundedness.

Proof.

For each p|qp\mid q, the trace function tℱpt_{\mathcal{F}_{p}} decomposes by (6.7) into a sum of at most rk⁡(ℱp)≤cond(ℱp)≤cond(𝓕)\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{F}_{p})\leq\cond(\mathcal{F}_{p})\leq\cond(\text{\boldmath${\mathcal{F}}$}) trace functions of isotypic admissible sheaves, and therefore n↦t⁡(n,q)n\mapsto t(n;q) decomposes into a sum of at most Cω⁡(q)C^{\omega(q)} functions, each of which is an admissible trace function modulo qq associated to isotypic admissible sheaves. Moreover, if no ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} contains a polynomial phase of degree ≤d\leq d, then all isotypic components share this property (in particular, since d≥1d\geq 1 for both statements, each component is also a Fourier sheaf). Thus we may assume without loss of generality that each ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} is isotypic.

We start with the proof of (6.21). By (4.12) we have

|∑nψN​(n)​t​(n,q)|\displaystyle\left|\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)t(n;q)\right| ≪q1/2+ε​(1+|N′|q)​suph∈ℤ/q​ℤ|FTq​(t⁡(h,q))|\displaystyle\ll q^{1/2+\varepsilon}\Bigl(1+\frac{|N^{\prime}|}{q}\Bigr)\sup_{h\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}|\mathrm{FT}_{q}(t(h;q))|
≪q1/2+ε​(1+Nq)​suph∈ℤ/q​ℤ|FTq​(t⁡(h,q))|\displaystyle\ll q^{1/2+\varepsilon}\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)\sup_{h\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}}|\mathrm{FT}_{q}(t(h;q))|

for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, where N′=∑nψN​(n)N^{\prime}=\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n). By Lemma 4.4, (6.19) and the definition of the Fourier transform, we have

FTq​(t⁡(⋅,q))​(h)=∏p|qFTp​(t⁡(⋅,p))​(qp¯​h).\mathrm{FT}_{q}(t(\cdot;q))(h)=\prod_{p|q}\mathrm{FT}_{p}(t(\cdot;p))(\overline{q_{p}}h).

Since t⁡(⋅,p)=tℱpt(\cdot;p)=t_{\mathcal{F}_{p}} is the trace function of a Fourier sheaf, we have

|FTp(t(⋅;p))(qp¯h)|≤10cond(ℱp)2≤10cond(𝓕)2|\mathrm{FT}_{p}(t(\cdot;p))(\overline{q_{p}}h)|\leq 10\cond(\mathcal{F}_{p})^{2}\leq 10\cond(\text{\boldmath${\mathcal{F}}$})^{2}

for all hh by (6.9) (or Corollary 6.6 applied to the sheaves ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} and ℒep​(−qp¯​x)\mathcal{L}_{e_{p}(-\overline{q_{p}}x)}). Combining these bounds, we obtain (6.21).

The proof of (6.22) follows closely that of (4.20). It is sufficient to prove this bound in the case r≤sr\leq s. We may also assume that r≤N≤sr\leq N\leq s, since, otherwise, the result follows either from the trivial bound or (6.21). Then, denoting K:=⌊N/r⌋K:=\lfloor N/r\rfloor, we write

∑nψN​(n)​t​(n,q)=1K​∑n∑k=1KψN​(n+k​r)​t​(n+k​r,q).\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)t(n;q)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\psi_{N}(n+kr)t(n+kr;q).

Since q=r​sq=rs, we have

t⁡(n+k​r,q)=t⁡(n,r)​t​(n+k​r,s),t(n+kr;q)=t(n;r)t(n+kr;s),

where

t⁡(n,r)=∏p|rt⁡(n,p),t⁡(n,s)=∏p|st⁡(n,p)t(n;r)=\prod_{p|r}t(n;p),\quad\quad t(n;s)=\prod_{p|s}t(n;p)

are admissible trace functions modulo rr and ss, respectively. Hence

|∑nψN​(n)​t​(n,q)|\displaystyle\Bigl|\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)t(n;q)\Bigr| ≪1K​∑n|∑k=1KψN​(n+k​r)​t​(n+k​r,s)|\displaystyle\ll\frac{1}{K}\sum_{n}\Bigl|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\psi_{N}(n+kr)t(n+kr;s)\Bigr|
≪N1/2K​(∑n|∑k=1KψN​(n+k​r)​t​(n+k​r,s)|2)1/2\displaystyle\ll\frac{N^{1/2}}{K}\Bigl(\sum_{n}\Bigl|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\psi_{N}(n+kr)t(n+kr;s)\Bigr|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}
≪N1/2K​(∑1≤k,l≤KA⁡(k,l))1/2,\displaystyle\ll\frac{N^{1/2}}{K}\Bigl(\sum_{1\leq k,l\leq K}A(k,l)\Bigr)^{1/2},

where

A⁡(k,l)=∑nψN​(n+k​r)​ψN​(n+l​r)¯​t​(n+k​r,s)​t⁡(n+l​r,s)¯.A(k,l)=\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n+kr)\overline{\psi_{N}(n+lr)}t(n+kr;s)\overline{t(n+lr;s)}.

The diagonal contribution satisfies

∑1≤k≤KA⁡(k,k)≪qε​K​N\sum_{1\leq k\leq K}A(k,k)\ll q^{\varepsilon}KN

for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, where the implied constant depends on cond(𝓕)\cond(\text{\boldmath${\mathcal{F}}$}).

Instead of applying (6.21) for the off-diagonal terms, it is slightly easier to just apply (4.12). For given k≠lk\neq l, since k​rkr, l​r≪Nlr\ll N, the sequence ΨN​(n)=ψN​(n+k​r)​ψN​(n+l​r)¯\Psi_{N}(n)=\psi_{N}(n+kr)\overline{\psi_{N}(n+lr)} satisfies the assumptions of (4.12). Denoting

we obtain

by (4.12) (since N≤sN\leq s). We have

with sp=s/ps_{p}=s/p. For p|k−lp\mid k-l, we use the trivial bound

and for p∤k−lp\nmid k-l, we have

FTp​(w⁡(⋅,p))​(sp¯​h)=1p1/2​∑x∈𝔽pt⁡(x+k​r,p)​t⁡(x+l​r,p)¯​ep​(sp¯​h​x)≪1\mathrm{FT}_{p}(w(\cdot;p))(\overline{s_{p}}h)=\frac{1}{p^{1/2}}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}t(x+kr;p)\overline{t(x+lr;p)}e_{p}(\overline{s_{p}}hx)\ll 1

by the change of variable x↦x+k​q1x\mapsto x+kq_{1} and (6.13), which holds for ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} by our assumptions. In all cases, the implied constant depends only on cond(ℱp)\cond(\mathcal{F}_{p}). Therefore we have

and summing over k≠lk\neq l, we derive

≪qε​N1/2K​(K1/2​N1/2+s1/4​K)\displaystyle\ll\frac{q^{\varepsilon}N^{1/2}}{K}(K^{1/2}N^{1/2}+s^{1/4}K)

which gives the desired conclusion (6.22). ∎

Remark 6.23.

Similarly to Remark 4.15, one can iterate the above argument and conclude that, for any l≥1l\geq 1, and any factorization q=q1⋯qlq=q_{1}\cdots q_{l}

|∑nψN​(n)​t​(n,q)|≪qε​((∑i=1l−1N1−1/2i​qi1/2i)+N1−1/2l−1​ql1/2l),\left|\sum_{n}\psi_{N}(n)t(n;q)\right|\ll q^{\varepsilon}\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{l-1}N^{1-1/2^{i}}q_{i}^{1/2^{i}}\right)+N^{1-1/2^{l-1}}q_{l}^{1/2^{l}}\right),

assuming that N<qN<q and the ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} do not contain any polynomial phase of degree ≤l\leq l.

Specializing Proposition 6.20 to the functions in Theorem 6.17, we conclude:
